  occurrence in the walk that "The name" gives below. No declared name
  starts with a digit, so it equals the name of no recursive type, and
  it uses no name of the author's.
- **What a recursive type is, precisely.** The unit is a declaration with
  its type arguments: an `interface` or a type alias of one module and,
  for a generic declaration, the types it is instantiated with. Two
  references name one unit where they resolve to the same declaration
  with equal type arguments. An alias whose body is nothing but a
  reference to another interface or alias, with or without type
  arguments, is no unit of its own: a reference to it is resolved to the
  unit its body names before anything else is decided, so
  `type Items = Tree<string>` stands for `Tree` with the argument
  `string`. A unit is recursive where expanding the body of its
  declaration, with the arguments substituted, meets a reference to the
  same unit, at any depth and through any number of other declarations,
  and through a handle, a `Default`, a scope wrapper or a label
  annotation as through a property, an element type or a member of a
  union. The test ends, because a recursive reference of the subset
  passes the parameters of its declaration unchanged
  (`language-subset.md` §7.3). Every unit on a cycle is recursive, so two
  declarations that refer to each other are two recursive types. A
  declaration that refers to a recursive type and that no path leads
  back to is not recursive: it is written in place, with a `$ref` where
  it names the recursive one.
- **What the member holds, and what refers to it.** The member of a
  recursive unit is the schema of its declaration's body with the
  arguments substituted, written as any type is. Every reference to a
  recursive unit is a `$ref`: the reference that closes the cycle, each
  other reference inside the member, and each reference from outside,
  the first one that a walk from the schema's root meets included. A
  type of the subset reaches itself only through a reference by name to
  an interface or an alias, since a type written in place has no name by
  which it could refer to itself. So every recursive type has a
  declaration, and no name is made up for one that has none. The
  compiler's type checker therefore keeps, for a reference to a declared
  type, the declaration and the type arguments it resolved to, and for a
  reference that closes a cycle it keeps that pair where it would
  otherwise expand the body. The schema writer takes the member's name
  and the target of each `$ref` from that pair.
- **The name** is the name the declaration gives the interface or the
  alias in its own module, without type arguments, whatever name an
  import of another module binds it to. Where
  one schema has two recursive types of one declared name, two
  declarations of two modules or two instantiations of one generic
  declaration, the first keeps the name and each later one has the name
  followed by `_2`, `_3` and so on. The order is that of first
  occurrence in a walk of the schema's root type, depth first, with the
  properties of an object in the order of their declaration and the
  members of a union in the order the mapping writes them. So the name
  of a type can differ between two schemas, and no rule compares names
  across schemas.
- **The documents.** The compiler emits a schema split as
  `decomposeSchema` (`runtime/runner/src/schema-decompose.ts`) splits
  one. The recursive types that reach each other are one document, of
  the form `{ "$defs": { ... } }` with those types as its members, which
  refer to each other by `#/$defs/<Name>`. Every reference to a member
  from outside that document is
  `{ "$ref": "cid:<hash>#/$defs/<Name>" }` with the document's hash.
  A member that reaches no member that reaches it back is a document
  of its own, which holds the member's schema and not its name, and a
  reference to it is `{ "$ref": "cid:<hash>" }`: `decomposeSchema`
  makes each definition that stands alone a document. That is every
  member that provisional decision P7 adds, except one that holds a
  `$ref` to a recursive type and stands inside that type's member; such
  a member is in the document of the cycle, under its ordinal. So the
  ordinal of a member that stands alone is in no emitted document and
  in no hash.
  What remains of the schema is its root document.
- **The hash.** Each document is hashed by the rule of section 1.2, which
  is the hash `decomposeSchema` gives it. A member of the plan that
  names a schema holds the root reference of the split
  (`DecomposedSchema.rootRef`) without its `cid:` prefix. That is the
  hash of the root document. Where the root type is itself recursive
  and nothing is written beside the reference to it, the split has no
  root document, and the member holds the hash of the type's document
  followed by `#/$defs/<Name>`.

The type each member is the schema of:

| Member | The type |
| --- | --- |
| `Plan.argumentSchema`, `Plan.resultSchema` | The argument type and the result type the pattern declares, or the checker infers |
| `StateCell.schema`, and `schema` of a `createCell` site | The value type of the cell constructor. For a `StateCell` whose declaration gives it a first value that is a constant, with that value as the default of the schema (section 1.3) |
| `Child.argumentSchema`, `Child.resultSchema` | The types the callee's type declares: for a compiled callee, its `Plan.argumentSchema` and `Plan.resultSchema` |
| `Binding.eventSchema`, `Binding.stateSchema` | The event type and the state type of the handler, or of the factory's type. The event type of a `handler(...)` is its first type argument or the annotation of its event parameter. That of an `action` is its first type argument or the annotation of its parameter, as in `action<{ index: number }>(...)`. That of an inline event handler is the type the checker gives its parameter: its annotation, or without one the type that the attribute's position expects (`language-subset.md` §7.6), which exists where the attribute is a path of the argument of a pattern that declares a stream there. An `on*` attribute of a host element declares no event type. *Assumed* (section 8, question 82): an inline handler written there without an annotation, or without a parameter, has the event type `unknown` |
| `Slot.schema` | The type under which the slot's reader observes the path (below) |
| `HandleReads.envelope` | The read envelope `footprint-analysis.md` §7.3 defines: the handle's value type, narrowed to the paths and classes some read through the handle may observe, with the label annotations of the paths it admits |

**The schema of a slot.** `Slot.schema` is the type the reader has at the
slot's path. For a slot of `Body.reads` it is the type the body declares
for the formal input the slot is in, at the path below it: the parameter
type of an authored function or a `lift`, the event type and the state
type of a handler. For a slot that expression code or a promoted
`computed` reads, and for a capture of a `computed` that is a body, it
is the static type the checker gives the expression that reads the path.
The type is the same for every class of slot at the path: the class says
what is observed, and the schema what the position can hold. Two reads
of one root and path in one class under two types are two entries of
`Plan.slots`, which differ in `schema` alone. They are bound to one
address and have one label, because the schema is no part of a slot's
key (section 1.2). Three rules read the type: whether a `shape` slot is
in place (section 2.5), whether a `value` slot above a handle reads
through it (section 3.11), and what the runtime validates a value
against before code sees it (section 5.2).

**Code.** Four members address code.

- `Cone.code` is the hash of the record `{ source }`, where `source` is
  the text of the cone's value function as the emitted value-code module
  holds it, from the first character of the function to the last, with
  the text of each emitted helper function it calls that is not the
  entry of another cone appended in the order of first use. The emitter
  has to be deterministic: one source and one compiler build give one
  text.
- `CompiledPattern.valueCode` is the hash of the record `{ source }` over
  the whole text of the emitted value-code module. The module does not
  hold the hash of the plan, so the plan, which holds every `Cone.code`,
  can be hashed after the module is emitted, and `CompiledPattern` after
  both.
- `Body.code` identifies a sandboxed body by the module that declares it
  and the binding it is declared at. *Assumed* (section 8, question 54):
  it is the hash of the record `{ module, binding }`. `module` is the
  content-addressed identity the loader gives the module the body's
  function is written in, the one `computeModuleIdentities`
  (`runtime/runner/src/sandbox/module-record-compiler.ts`) computes
  today from the module's source and the identities of the modules it
  imports. `binding` is the path of the function's binding in that
  module: the name of the `const` for a handler, a `lift` or an authored
  function declared at module scope, and for a function written in
  place, a `computed`, an `action` or an inline event handler, the name
  of the enclosing pattern's binding followed by the `within` steps and
  the `name` of the use (section 1.3). This is the pair that
  `writeAuthorizedBy` verifies today (`moduleIdentity` and `bindingPath`
  in `resolveProvenanceImplementationIdentity`,
  `runtime/runner/src/cfc/implementation-identity.ts`). It covers every
  authored function the body can call, because those are in the module
  or in a module it imports.
- An entry of `Plan.patterns` identifies a pattern by the module that
  declares it and the binding it is declared at. *Assumed* (section 8,
  question 64): it is the hash of a record `{ module, binding }` formed as
  the record of `Body.code` is. `module` is the identity of the module the
  `pattern(...)` call is written in. `binding` is the path of the
  pattern's binding in that module: the name of the `const` the call
  initializes; `default` for a call that is the operand of
  `export default`; and for an inline `pattern(...)`, which no `const`
  names, the binding of the enclosing pattern followed by the `within`
  steps and the name of the site that instantiates it (section 1.3). A
  pattern and a sandboxed body declared at one binding cannot occur, so
  the two kinds of record do not collide. The identity of a pattern
  changes when anything in its module, or in a module that one imports,
  changes, as `Body.code` does (section 8, question 54). It does not
  change with the patterns that compile it in, so one pattern has one
  identity in every plan that holds its code.

Each of the four records is hashed by the rule of section 1.2. `source`
is the text as one string. `module` is the string
`computeModuleIdentities` returns, which `computeModuleHashes`
(`runtime/runner/src/harness/module-identity.ts`) forms and which has no
algorithm tag. `binding` is an array of strings, one per step of the
path. The runtime has no equivalent of `Cone.code` or of
`CompiledPattern.valueCode` today, because it has no emitted value code,
and it holds the pair of `Body.code` without hashing it: `moduleIdentity`
and `bindingPath` are members of the `ImplementationIdentity` of kind
`verified` (`runtime/runner/src/cfc/types.ts`) that a `TransformedBy`
atom carries as its `identity` (`mintTransformedBy` in
`runtime/runner/src/cfc/input-witness.ts`). The identity also holds
`symbol`, the name the module exports the function's builder under, or
the name `hoistBuilderCalls`
(`base/ts-transformers/src/transformers/builder-call-hoisting.ts`) gives a
builder call it moves to module scope, such as the callback of a
`computed` written in a pattern
(`resolveProvenanceImplementationIdentity` in
`runtime/runner/src/cfc/implementation-identity.ts`, from what
`recordVerifiedProvenance` in
`runtime/runner/src/harness/verified-provenance.ts` recorded). An atom
pattern matches a record by the members it names
(`runtime/runner/src/cfc/atom-pattern.ts`), and the exchange rules of
`patterns/examples/cfc-exchange-rules/` name a function by
`moduleIdentity` and `symbol`. No atom the runtime mints today names a
pattern: a `TransformedBy` atom names the function whose run wrote, and a
pattern's own function builds a graph and writes nothing under a
transaction's identity. *Assumed* (section 8, questions 54, 63 and 64):
the records as given here, and that a `TransformedBy` atom of the compiled
path carries the hash.

`Child.callee.compiled` and `Closure.pattern` are the identity of a
compiled pattern (section 1.2), so a pattern is compiled after the
patterns it names in this way. `CompiledPattern.compiler` is given by
the build. `WriterPolicy.body` is `Body.code` of the handler the
annotation's binding names: the compiler resolves `typeof b` to the
declaration of `b` and forms the record from it, whether or not the plan
being emitted has a `Body` for that handler.

**Declared labels.** `Slot.declared` is read from the annotations of the
type `Slot.schema` is the schema of, taken from the root of the slot's
formal input, or of the declaration the root names, down to the slot's
path, and combined as `language-subset.md` §8.3 combines the annotations
on a path. The values are the label arguments in the canonical form
`language-subset.md` §8.5 gives them.

- `declared.confidentiality` is the combined `confidentiality` list at
  the path. For a `value` slot over a subtree it is joined with the
  lists of the annotated nodes below the path, since the slot observes
  them. Where the type below the path is recursive, each annotated node
  is taken once.
- `declared.integrity` is the combined `integrity` list at the path. The
  nodes below the path add nothing: the integrity of a subtree read
  whole is a meet.
- A handle type on the way is two nodes: the handle, with the
  annotations written around it, and its value type, with the
  annotations written inside it. A slot whose path crosses the hop
  combines both, the handle's first.
- A slot at a path with no such annotation at or above it has no
  `declared` member, and one with an annotation of one dimension alone
  has that member alone.
- Where two nodes on the path declare `integrity` differently the type
  is refused (`cfc-label:conflict`, `language-subset.md` §8.3), so the
  combined list is the list of whichever node declares it.
- *Assumed* (section 8, question 55): an `identity` slot and a `shape`
  slot in place have no `declared` member, because they observe the
  reference stored at the position, whose label is a pointer label, and
  the annotation declares the label of the value.

**Constraints.** `Plan.constraints` is built after the templates, from
the annotations of two sets of schemas (section 4.4 has the keys).

- **At a write target.** For each `WriteEdge` and each kept `Output`, the
  compiler takes the type at the written path: of the `StateCell.schema`
  for a `state` target, of the handle's value type at the target's
  `path` for a `handle` target, of `Child.argumentSchema` for an
  `argument` target, of the `createCell` site's schema for a `created`
  target, of the built-in's request type for a `request` target, and of
  `Plan.resultSchema` for a kept output. The annotations combined at
  that path give a `writerFit` constraint where a `confidentiality` is
  declared, a `writer` constraint where a `writeAuthorizedBy` or a
  `writePolicyAnyOf` is, and a `writeFloor` constraint where a
  `requiredIntegrity` is (*assumed*, below). Each is listed in the
  `constraints` of that edge or output, and a kept output has all three
  kinds as a write edge has. An interim output has no declared type and
  no constraint.

  Eight points complete the rule.

  - **The type at each target.** The compiler reads the annotations from
    the type, and needs no schema hash to form a constraint.

    | Target | The type |
    | --- | --- |
    | `state` | The type argument of the cell constructor. A constructor with no type argument has the type the checker infers from the initial value, which has no annotation, so the cell has no constraint |
    | `created`, naming a `createCell` site | The same, for the constructor at the site |
    | `created`, naming a `bind` site | The event type of the handler the site binds, the type `Binding.eventSchema` is the schema of |
    | `handle` | The handle's value type, as the body that holds the edge declares it |
    | `argument` | The argument type of the callee, the type `Child.argumentSchema` is the schema of: the declared argument type of a callee the compiler resolved, and the argument type of the factory type otherwise. A child a site of a body instantiates has it as a child of the reactive tier has |
    | `request`, of an effect | The type of the parameter the API declares for the built-in (`base/api/index.ts`), at the path of the request |
    | `request`, of a `wish` | `WishParams` |
    | `request`, of a `reduce`, at `initial` | The accumulator type |
    | A kept output | The result type the pattern declares, or the checker infers |

    A `WriteEnvelope` and an `anchors` target have no declared type and
    no constraint. No request type the API declares has a label
    annotation today, so no `request` target has a constraint of this
    kind.

  - **The written path** is the target's `path`, or `Output.path`, read
    in the type named above, with `*` taking the element type of an
    array and the value type of a record. A `push`, a `pushAll` and an
    `addUnique` have the target path `*` below the list
    (`footprint-analysis.md` §6.1), so the annotations of the element
    type apply to them. The annotations are combined from the root of
    that type down to the written path (`language-subset.md` §8.3). For
    a `handle` target the root is the handle's value type, as the body
    that holds the edge declares it, and the annotations written around
    the handle type do not apply: they are about the position that holds
    the handle.
  - **A write floor.** *Assumed* (section 8, question 15): a
    `requiredIntegrity` annotation combined at the written path gives a
    `writeFloor` constraint with the annotation's patterns, listed in
    the `constraints` of the edge or the output as the two above are. A
    kept output is a write to a path of the result, so the floor
    declared in the result type applies to it as the floor of a cell
    applies to a write edge. `language-subset.md` §8.6 states the same
    assumption.
  - **Two writer annotations on one path.** A `writeAuthorizedBy` and a
    `writePolicyAnyOf` are two keys, so a path can combine one of each
    from two nodes, as an element type under `WritePolicyAnyOf` with a
    property under `WriteAuthorizedBy` does. Each annotation gives a
    `writer` constraint of its own, and the write has to satisfy every
    one. That is what the runtime does today: `writeAuthorizedByReason`
    and `writePolicyAnyOfReason` are tested one after the other in
    `runtime/runner/src/cfc/prepare.ts`.
  - **A `uiContract` with no writer.** A `uiContract` annotation at a
    node that declares no `writeAuthorizedBy`, which is what
    `TrustedActionUiContract` gives, is a `writer` constraint with one
    `WriterPolicy` that has the `uiContract` and no `body`. Any body may
    make the write, and the event has to satisfy the contract (section
    4.4).
  - **An annotation below the written path.** A write of a whole value
    writes every path below it. So each annotated node below the written
    path gives its constraints to the edge or the output too, tested on
    the template of the edge or the output, unless the plan has a finer
    edge or entry at or below that node, which then has them. Without
    this a body could replace a record whole where a policy guards one
    of its properties. Today the prepare step tests every annotated
    entry of the target's schema (`cfcSchemaEntries` in
    `runtime/runner/src/cfc/schema-label-view.ts`).
  - **Which record lists the constraint.** A write edge is a member of
    `Body.writes` or of `Cone.writes`, and the constraint is listed in
    its `constraints`, whatever the target. For a `state`, a `handle`
    and a `created` target that is the edge of the body or the cone that
    writes. For an `argument` target it is the edge, one per path of the
    argument, of the cone that computes the path, or of the body whose
    site instantiates the child. For a `request` target it is the edge
    of the cone that computes the path of the request, or of the body
    whose site requests the effect. For a kept output it is
    `Output.constraints`. An `anchors` target has no declared type and
    no constraint of this kind.
  - **A writer that is no body.** A `writer` constraint on a kept output
    or on a write edge of `Cone.writes` that expression code computes
    has no `Body.code` to compare, so no alternative with a `body`
    admits the write. An alternative without a `body` is not affected.
    Where the template of the output or the edge is a `derive` by a
    body at its root, that body is the writer. A root that is an
    `output` node is followed to the root of the template it names, so
    an output that passes the result of a body on unchanged has that
    body as its writer. The compiler decides it once per output.
- **At an input.** For each use of a body, the compiler takes each
  `requiredIntegrity` and `maxConfidentiality` annotation of the types
  of the body's formal inputs, and of the read envelopes of its
  handles, and forms one constraint from it that lists the entries of
  the body's footprint whose path overlaps the annotated path
  (`ConstraintInputs`, section 4.4). A constraint that lists nothing is
  not emitted. The constraint is listed in the `constraints` of every
  write edge of the body, and of every output whose template has a
  `derive` by that body: those are the writes the body's inputs flow
  into. The `derive` can be anywhere in the output's template: under a
  `select`, a `fold` or a `pick`, in the template of an output that an
  `output` node names, and in the template of an entry of
  `Body.computed` of another body. So an output that passes a body's
  result on through a further cone lists the constraint too. The rule
  follows `output` nodes (section 3.2, "A rule over a template"), and
  the compiler computes it per output, once each: the input constraints
  of an output are those of the bodies of the `derive` nodes that its
  own template holds, with the input constraints of each output that an
  `output` node of the template names.

  Three points complete the rule.

  - **The types read.** The type of a formal input is the one the body
    declares: the parameter type of an authored function or a `lift`,
    the event type and the state type of a handler. A capture of a
    `computed`, of an `action` or of an inline event handler has no
    declared formal input, and its type is the static type the checker
    gives the captured expression, the type `Slot.schema` is the schema
    of.
  - **An annotation behind a hop.** An annotation written inside the
    value type of a handle is behind the hop of that handle. An entry at
    or above the handle overlaps such a path only where the entry reads
    through the hop: a `value` entry that reads through the handle
    (section 3.11), an entry whose own path continues below the handle,
    and an entry of `Body.handles`. An `identity` entry and a `shape`
    entry in place observe the reference stored at the position and
    nothing behind it, so they do not overlap the path, and the
    constraint does not list them. A body that holds a handle and reads
    nothing through it is therefore not held to a requirement declared
    on the content of the handle's cell, as it is not today, when it
    makes no read of that cell. An annotation written around the handle
    type is in front of the hop, and it lists every entry at an
    overlapping path, whatever its class.
  - **A body that writes nothing.** A body with no write edge, and with
    no output whose template has a `derive` by it, has no constraint
    from its inputs: none is emitted, and no compile-time check is made.
    An input constraint guards writes, and today's gate tests the reads
    before an overlapping write (`verifyInputRequirements`), so it tests
    nothing where there is none.
- **At an input of expression code.** *Assumed* (section 8, question
  59): expression code and a promoted `computed` are constrained as a
  body is. A `requiredIntegrity` or a `maxConfidentiality` annotation of
  the type a slot of the cone is read under (`Slot.schema`) gives a
  constraint that lists the slots of `Cone.slots` whose path overlaps
  the annotated path, in `ConstraintInputs.slots`. It is listed in the
  `constraints` of every output and every write edge of the cone whose
  template reaches one of the listed slots. "Reaches" follows an
  `output` node into the template it names, and whether an output
  reaches a slot is computed once per output (section 3.2, "A rule over
  a template").

Equal constraints are one entry of `Plan.constraints`.

**The compile-time checks.** Each `cfc-flow:*` diagnostic of
`language-subset.md` §10.5 evaluates one kind of constraint on declared
labels, by the rule of section 4.4, "When a constraint is checked".

| Diagnostic | Evaluated on |
| --- | --- |
| `cfc-flow:write-policy` | A `writer` constraint of a static write edge: the `Body.code` of the body whose record holds the edge against the `body` of each `WriterPolicy`. It needs the resolution of the bindings the policy names and no label |
| `cfc-flow:writer-fit` | A `writerFit` constraint: the template of the edge or the output, with each `slot` node replaced by `Slot.declared.confidentiality`, against the confidentiality declared at the target |
| `cfc-flow:write-floor` | A `writeFloor` constraint: the same template, with each `slot` node replaced by `Slot.declared.integrity` |
| `cfc-flow:max-confidentiality`, `cfc-flow:required-integrity` | An input constraint: the `declared` member of each slot it lists, and for an entry of `Body.computed` the entry's template with its `slot` nodes replaced in the same way |
| `cfc-flow:ui-contract` | A `writer` constraint whose alternative has a `uiContract`, and the bindings of the plan that name the handler (section 4.4) |

Section 4.4 defines the relations each check tests ("The relations a
constraint tests") and, per diagnostic, the cases the compiler reports
and the cases it leaves to the runtime ("What the compiler decides"). A
template is evaluated on declared labels only where every `slot` node
it reaches has the `declared` member of the dimension tested, on every
selection, and it has no `dynamic` node, no `fold` and no `pick`. Both
conditions follow `output` nodes, and the evaluation of an output's
template on declared labels is made once per output and reused at every
`output` node that names it (section 3.2, "A rule over a template"). An
input constraint is evaluated only where it lists no entry of
`Body.handles`. In every other case the diagnostic is not reported and
the constraint is checked at instantiation. One case is large: an
`identity` slot has no `declared` member, so `cfc-flow:writer-fit` and
`cfc-flow:write-floor` are not decided for any write of a body that
holds a handle (section 4.4, "What the compiler decides").

`cfc-flow:write-policy` needs no hash. Two bodies have one `Body.code`
exactly where they are one declaration, so the compiler compares the
declaration the policy's binding reference resolves to
(`language-subset.md` §8.5) with the declaration of the body whose
record holds the write edge. A write made by an authored function the
body calls is an edge of the body's record
(`footprint-analysis.md` §3.6), so it is checked as the body's. A
policy written through `WritePolicyAnyOf` or a trusted-action alias has
one `WriterPolicy` per alternative, and the edge passes where one of
them names the body.

## 2. Slots and observation classes

### 2.1 The classes

A slot is one input at one path observed in one way. The class says what the
computation learns.

| Class | What is learned | Typical source construct |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | The content at the path, recursively | Reading a scalar; passing a subtree to a body that reads all of it |
| `shape` | That the path exists, and its kind | `x !== undefined`, `typeof x`, truthiness of an object |
| `enumeration` | Which children a container has, their order and count | `.length`, iteration, `map` membership |
| `identity` | Which reference sits at the path, not what it refers to | Passing a link on, comparing two cells |
| `labelMetadata` | The label stored for the path | `principalOf`, `inspectConfLabel` (section 2.4) |

These are the observations of §4.6.3 (`04-label-representation.md`), which
defines `shape`, `value` and `iterate` entries per path and states: "Static
child access `p/sel` is navigation plus observations at `p/sel`; it does
**not** implicitly materialize or declassify the parent `p`." That rule is
what makes a slot per path meaningful: reading `message.body` is a `value`
slot at `body` and no observation of `message`.

`identity` is §4.6.3's standalone reference-identity read, which consumes "the
reference scalar's `value(p)`" and "never any observation of the referenced
target".

### 2.2 Mapping to the runtime's vocabulary

The runtime stores labels as envelope entries with an `observes` class and
resolves a read by its shape. The types are `LabelObservationClass` in
`runtime/runner/src/cfc/label-view-core.ts` (`"value" | "shape" | "enumerate"
| "followRef"`) and `ReadObservationShape` in
`runtime/runner/src/cfc/observation-classes.ts`
(`"value" | "shape" | "followRef"`). The table `CONSUMED_CLASSES` there says
which entry classes each read shape consumes.

| Slot class | Read shape it resolves as | Entry classes consumed | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | `value` | `value`, `shape`, `enumerate` | At the slot's path, recursively |
| `shape` | `shape` | `shape`, `enumerate` | At the slot's path |
| `shape`, with `inPlace` | `followRef` where the position holds a link, `shape` where it does not | `followRef`; or `shape`, `enumerate` | At the slot's path, without continuing through a link stored there (section 2.5) |
| `enumeration` | `shape` | `shape`, `enumerate` | At the container's path |
| `identity` | `followRef` | `followRef` | At the slot's path, and for a `resolved` slot at every link resolution follows from there |

The label of a slot is defined as **the label a journaled read of that shape
at that address consumes today**: the entries
`consumedEntriesForRead` selects and `labelForConsumedEntries` joins
(`runtime/runner/src/cfc/consumed-label.ts`), resolved as
[CFC observation classes](../cfc-observation-classes.md) §4 describes. This
definition is what the precision comparison in section 3 rests on. A template
joins the labels of a set of slots, and each of those labels is the label one
read contributes to the per-transaction join today.

**The label of a slot of root `index`.** The slot has no stored address:
its value is the position of the current element, which the runtime
computes from the order the collection iterates. Its label is defined by
rule and not by a read. By ruling, it is the label of the collection's
own array: the length of the array, and which link each position holds.
It holds nothing of what the links point to. It is the label of the
whole array, and no narrower label is formed for the positions up to
the element's own. A `slot` node that names the slot instantiates to
that label.

The label of the array is the join of two parts.

- **The membership the collection iterates,** as the table of section
  3.2 gives it by `Collection.source`. For a collection over a slot it
  is the label of the `enumeration` slot at the source's path, which
  consumes the `shape` and `enumerate` entries at the array's own path.
  No entry below the array is in it.
- **The root of every position** of the array the collection iterates,
  observed in place: the label of a `shape` slot with `inPlace` at the
  position (the table above). Where the position holds a link, that is
  the `followRef` entries at the position, which is the label of which
  reference the position holds. Where it holds a value in place, it is
  the `shape` and `enumerate` entries at the position, which is the
  label of whether the position holds anything and of what kind. The
  slot stops at the position (section 2.5), so nothing of the cell a
  link leads to is in it, and no `value` entry is.

For an array the instance computed, a position has no stored address
until the collection is kept, and the root of a position takes the
producing template, as section 3.6 gives the element's root slots.
Section 3.7 gives the label of the array of a derived collection.

The join is a join in the sense of section 3.2. Its confidentiality is
the join of the parts, its integrity is the meet of the integrity of
the parts, and it is the same label for every key of the collection, so
one transaction forms it once per collection. No rule gives a position
an integrity of its own beside that meet.

An entry of origin `link` at a position is not in the second part. It
holds what the reference at the position declares, which for a link to a
cell repeats the label of the cell's type ("The `link` entry of a handle
that is only passed on is not in it", below). That is a label of what
the link points to, and by the ruling the label of the index holds none
of it. Where such an entry holds more than the target's declaration, it
is left out under the assumption of section 8, question 81.

The position of a key is a function of the length of the array and of
which element part each position holds. For a position that holds a
link, the element part is the identity of the cell linked, and the
second part above is its label. Two more cases are ruled.

- **A position that holds a plain value in place.** Its element part is
  derived from the value (section 1.3), so which key stands at which
  position is a function of the values. By ruling the label of the
  array holds the root `shape` of such a position and not its `value`. Deciding which key an element has is the
  runtime's observation and not the body's (section 1.3), and a node
  that reads the index is given a number and no value. A node that
  reads the element as well carries the element's label by its own
  slots.
- **A derived collection.** Which elements the result of a `filter` or
  a `flatMap` holds, and at which position, was computed, and section
  3.7 gives the label of that array. It includes what the predicates
  read, which can be values behind links of the source. That is the
  label of which elements the array holds and not of what its links
  point to. By ruling the label is formed whole, as for a stored
  array.

**The label of an `identity` slot.** By ruling, a handle that a body passes
on without reading through it adds nothing of the label of its cell to what
the body writes. The label stays at the cell and reaches only a reader that
follows the handle. The definition above gives that rule, read as follows.

- **It is the label of the link.** The slot's label is what a `followRef`
  read consumes at the position that holds the reference: the path of the
  document the body was given the handle from, such as a path of the
  argument document or of a binding's state document, and each link crossed
  before that position (section 2.5). The entries a `followRef` read
  consumes are those of class `followRef`, which are the label a link was
  written with: the stamp of the run that wrote the link at that position
  (section 3.1). An entry that a schema declares with the class
  `followRef` at the position is a label declared for the reference
  itself, and it is consumed with them. The label says which cell the
  handle names, and under what label that was decided.
- **The position of a slot of root `element`.** A handler of an element
  body that is given the handle of its element has that state path bound
  to a slot of root `element`. By ruling, the callback of a per-element
  construct is a pattern, and labels flow through it per value (section
  3.6, "Labels flow per value"): the element has the label of its own
  slot of the collection and of what that slot holds. So the position
  that holds the reference is the element's position in the source
  collection. The slot's label is what a `followRef` read consumes
  there and at each link crossed below it. It holds nothing of what
  another position of the collection holds, and nothing of the
  collection's length or order.

  The runtime of today reads the slot at another position. Each run of
  an element callback is an instance with an argument document of its
  own, which holds the element at `element` as a link to the position
  in the source (`createRunInput` in
  `runtime/runner/src/builtins/map.ts`). The handler is given the handle
  from there, so the runtime reads at `element` of the argument document
  of the element's instance, and the link to the source position and
  each link below it are links crossed from there. The entries of class
  `followRef` at that position hold the join of the coordinator's
  transaction that set the element up (section 3.6, "Today, the
  argument document of an element"). The compiled path has no argument
  document per element, and the slot holds none of that join. The
  template is **tighter** there, deliberately (section 3.1, "The
  coordinator's join on an element's argument document").

  The link at `element` has an entry of origin `link` only where the
  schema that the stored link carries has a clause, and the entry then
  holds that clause (section 3.6). A clause that the source list
  declares for itself is not on it: such a clause is one entry of origin
  `declared` at the root of the list's document, with no class, and in
  the argument document it is in the coordinator's join, on the entries
  of origin `structure`. So two labels are told apart here. What the
  reference at the element's position declares is a `link` entry at
  that position in the source, and a slot that is `resolved` holds it
  by the rule below. The label that the declaration of the source
  collection gives the element is no `link` entry, and a `followRef`
  read at the position does not consume it. *Assumed* (section 8,
  question 85): where the slot is `resolved`, or the body reads or
  writes through the handle, the slot's label also holds that declared
  label: the entries of origin `declared` in the document that holds
  the element's position, at the position and above it, that a `shape`
  read at the position consumes.
- **The position of a handle an element body closes over.** A handle
  that the callback of a per-element construct captures is a slot or an
  output of the enclosing instance, as every captured outer value is
  (section 3.6). By the same ruling each captured value has its own
  label, and the slot is read at the captured place: the path of the
  enclosing instance's argument document, or the state cell, that holds
  the reference. Its label is the same for every element and holds
  nothing of the collection. The runtime of today gives a handler of an
  element body each captured handle from `params` of the element's
  argument document, which holds one link per captured cell to the path
  of the enclosing pattern's argument that holds it. The entries of
  class `followRef` at `params/*` hold the coordinator's join, and a
  handler that writes through a captured handle consumes them (section
  3.6). The slot of the compiled path holds none of that join.
- **The `link` entry of a handle that is only passed on is not in it.**
  The runtime stores, at the position of a link, an entry of origin `link`
  that holds what the reference declares (`prepareBoundaryCommitSteps` in
  `runtime/runner/src/cfc/prepare.ts`). The schema of a link to a cell is
  the cell's own, so that entry repeats the label the cell's type
  declares. By the ruling it is the label of the cell and stays out of
  the slot's label where the body neither reads nor writes through the
  handle and does not resolve it. *Assumed* (section 8, question 81):
  the same holds where the `link` entry holds more than the target's
  declaration.
- **The `link` entry of a handle the body resolves is in it.** A slot
  with `resolved` is read at the link: resolution starts from the
  reference at the position and follows it, and the runtime's
  transaction makes a `followRef` read of that position, which consumes
  the `link` entry with the other entries of class `followRef` there.
  The definition above therefore puts the entry in the slot's label,
  although the body reads no content through the handle. The case the
  stage 3 comparison observed is the handler `askToRetire` of
  `patterns/system/profile-picker/profile-picker.tsx`, which calls
  `spaceOf(profile)` on the handle of its element and sets a state cell
  (`spaceOf` in `runtime/runner/src/builder/space-access.ts` calls
  `resolveAsCell()`). Its transaction reads `element` of the argument
  document of the element's instance, the position in the list that the
  link there names, and the link below that position. What it stores
  for the write has the clause the input list declares. In the runs the
  prototype observed, the argument document of the element's instance
  has no entry of origin `link`, and the clause is on its entries of
  origin `structure`, the entry of class `followRef` at `*` among them,
  which is the coordinator's join. So that run does not show a `link`
  entry consumed, and the template is **equal** there by the assumption
  of question 85 above, which gives the slot the label the list
  declares for the element. Without that assumption the template has no
  clause and mints no atom (section 3.1, "A template with no clause
  beside the coordinator's join"). The rule of this item holds for every
  call that section 3.16 records
  with a resolved `identity` slot, and for a call it records as
  journaled, whose slot is not `resolved` and is named by a `dynamic`
  node of kind `link` or `space`: the run follows the reference there
  too. `equalLinks` has slots that are not resolved, follows nothing,
  and makes no read at either position (section 3.16), so a handle that
  a body only compares with it is treated as one that is only passed on
  (section 8, question 81).
- **Nothing of the target document is in it.** The slot is not resolved to
  the cell the reference leads to, and no entry of that cell's document
  joins it: not the `declared` entries that the cell's own type gives it,
  and not the `derived` and `structure` entries of what is written in the
  cell. A `declared` entry with no class of its own is one that a read of
  content consumes. A `followRef` read does not consume it, at the target
  or at the position (`readConsumesEntry` in
  `runtime/runner/src/cfc/observation-classes.ts`).
- **A `resolved` slot** joins the `followRef` entries of each further link
  that resolution follows (section 2.5), the `link` entry at each of
  them included, and nothing of the cell where resolution ends.
- **What brings the target's label in** is a read through the handle: a
  slot whose path continues past the reference, or a `dynamic` node
  (sections 2.5 and 3.10). A body that holds a handle in order to pass it
  on, to compare it, to resolve it, or to write through it has the
  `identity` slot in its template and no such read.

This is **equal** to today in the case the stage 3 comparison observed, in
`patterns/showcase/battleship/multiplayer/repro-minimal.tsx`. The handler
`joinAsP1` writes one input and passes the handles of that input and of a
second one to a child. Its transaction reads neither the position of the
second link in the argument document nor the document the link names, so
the runtime makes no observation for a handle that is only passed on, and
what it stored for the write, and for the links in the child's argument,
holds no clause of the second input. Where the link at the position was
itself written under a label, the slot has that stamp and the runtime's
join does not, and the template is looser by it; the comparison met no
such row.

Three consequences of the mapping:

- **`shape` and `enumeration` resolve alike.** The runtime has no entry class
  that separates a key-presence probe from an enumeration: a `shape` read at a
  container consumes its `enumerate` entries
  ([CFC observation classes](../cfc-observation-classes.md) §4). The plan
  keeps the two classes apart because the specification does (§4.6.3 gives a
  count-shaped read its own row), so that a runtime which later stores a
  separate count entry can resolve `enumeration` more narrowly without a
  change to compiled plans.
- **A `value` slot at a container covers its children.** It consumes what a
  recursive read consumes. Footprint analysis prefers narrower slots. Where
  it gives up, the slots it records cover the entries a precise analysis
  would have recorded (section 1.1, `Widening`): a `value` slot at the
  projection of a value it lost, which stands for the subtree below; slots
  at `*` for a key it could not name, which stand for every child, with
  the `enumeration` slot of the keyed container; and for a
  handle it lost, an entry of `Body.handles` whose envelope is the handle's
  whole declared type. On an input the instance computed, the wider entries
  are entries of `Body.computed`, and `Widening.computed` names them. This
  is the over-approximation the overview allows.
- **`identity` never reaches the target.** It observes which reference sits
  at the path, and its label is the label of the link there ("The label of
  an `identity` slot", above). What the reference refers to is read at a
  path that continues past it: by a slot whose path crosses the link, where
  the plan names the path (section 2.5), and by a `dynamic` template where
  it does not (section 3.10).

### 2.3 The stored form of an instantiated label

An instantiated label is stored as envelope entries of the existing shape
([CFC stored envelope](../cfc-stored-envelope.md)): `LabelMapEntry` with
`origin: "derived"` and an `observes` class. One kept output path produces the
entries the persist step of `prepareBoundaryCommitSteps`
(`runtime/runner/src/cfc/prepare.ts`) produces for a written path today:

- a `value` entry holding the instantiated label, replaced on overwrite;
- a `shape` entry holding its confidentiality, frozen at the path's creation
  (§8.12.8, `08-12-store-label-monotonicity.md`);
- for a kept collection, an `enumerate` entry at the container holding the
  instantiated membership template, and `*`-child entries for the element
  template where every element instantiates to the same label.

**A stored label is concrete.** By ruling (2026-11-19), what is stored is
the instantiated label: its clauses and atoms. A stored label is not a
symbolic reference to the labels of its sources that a reader resolves at
egress, so it does not follow a later change of a source's label, and a
reader needs no envelope of a source to evaluate it. A source whose label
changes reaches the stored label through re-instantiation alone
(section 4.1, "A label that changes alone").

**One entry for the elements of an array written whole.** Provisional
(P31 of the continuation plan). When an array is written whole and every
element of it is covered with one label, the runtime stores one entry at
the array's `*` path and none per element. An element written later with
that label adds no entry. An element written later with another label adds
an entry of its own at its position, and a read of that position consumes
the union of that entry and the `*` entry. A `splice` of the array removes
the `*` entry, and the elements then take the label of the list. Each of
the two limits gives a label equal to or wider than the label per element,
never a narrower one. The rule is the stored form of the `uniform` form of
section 4.2. Measured by milestone 4 of the integration, for a kept output
per element of a list: with one entry per element, the preparation of a
change of one element took 2.2, 16.8 and 157.5 ms at 100, 1,000 and 10,000
elements, because every commit encoded, hashed and compacted every entry;
with the one `*` entry, 0.6 to 0.8 ms at each size
([the integration plan](../../plans/compiled-pattern-language-integration.md),
"Milestone 4: labels from templates at commit"). In those fixtures the `*`
entries are stored for a list that is an array of plain values in place and
for one that is an array of references; the list that is the result of a
`map` stores none.

Declared entries (`origin: "declared"`) are unchanged: they come from the
schema, not from a template. The format of the stored bytes is a host
arrangement and does not change.

**A path that a write edge targets** has the same entries in the document
it is written in: a state cell, a cell reached through a handle, a created
cell. The `value` entry holds the instantiated template of the edge and is
replaced by each write. The `shape` entry holds the confidentiality of the
write that created the path, and a later write that replaces the value
leaves it as it is, at the written path and at each path below it that
still exists (§8.12.8). A write that removes a path and creates it again
mints the entry anew from its own label. So a reader of a written path
consumes, beside the label of the last write, the existence label of the
write that created the path, as it does today (section 3.1, "An existence
entry that an earlier write left"). *Assumed* (section 8, question 83): a
`shape` entry at a path that a write removed, such as a position beyond
the end of a list that became shorter, stays until the path is created
again, as it does in the runtime today.

**Several documents.** The keep set of an instance is stored in as many
documents as serve its readers. A kept subtree, such as a row of a kept
collection or a part of the rendered tree, can be stored in a document of
its own, a **part document**, with the place it has in the result holding a
link to it. Which subtrees are split off, how a part document is
identified, and what a reader of a part demands belong to
`execution-and-storage.md` (§4.10). Provisional (P20 of the continuation
plan): by the same section an array that is too large for one document is
stored as chunk documents, each a contiguous run of its entries, with a
list of storage links to the chunks at the place of the array. A chunk
list and a link to a chunk are storage links, a chunk's envelope is
complete for its paths as a part's is, and what follows holds for them as
for a part. Provisional (P27): a record with many members is stored in
chunks the same way, by ranges of member names, and its chunk list is
storage structure as an array's is. *Assumed* there: a bound in the chunk
list of a record is a member name and is read under the label of the
record's set of names. How the chunk of a key is found is open, with no
provisional decision (the continuation plan's question 299); until it is
decided, a runtime that does not hold an array's keys in memory reads the
array's chunks to resolve a reference by key. Chunked storage of a long
array is a requirement on the storage layer, which today's runtime has as
well; this design keeps of it the split points, the reference to a placed
collection (section 1.4, "Placed, and not observed"), and the bound that
the change of one row writes and delivers an amount that does not depend on
the length. A split changes neither a value nor a label when the following
hold.

- **The link is not a reference of the language.** The link from the result,
  or from one part to another, is a **storage link**, which the runtime
  writes and no pattern code holds. Resolving a path passes through it
  without observing it. It is never the reference an `identity` slot
  observes, it is not on a slot's chain (section 2.5), it gives an element
  no cell identity as a key (section 1.3), and a body that passes on a
  subtree which happens to be a part passes on what it would pass on if the
  subtree were stored in place. A reference to a kept path names the
  result cell and the path, whichever document stores the path.
- **The link carries no label.** A read that passes through a storage link
  consumes nothing for it. Every observation class at every kept path
  consumes what it would consume if the subtree were stored in place. A
  storage link to a part names the part document and holds nothing else:
  no path, no schema, no scope, and no label entry. Two labels concern the
  place a part
  has, and both are stored where a layout without the split stores them.
  Which rows a collection has is the `enumerate` entry of the collection's
  document, and that a row exists is the `shape` entry at the row's root,
  which is the root of the part.
- **Entries follow the paths they label.** The entries of a path inside a
  part document, the root of the part included, are stored in that
  document's envelope, at the path relative to the part's root: the `value`
  entry, the frozen `shape` entry, the `enumerate` and `*`-child entries of
  a collection inside the part, and the declared entries the result schema
  gives those paths. An entry at a path above the part, including the
  `enumerate` entry and the `*`-child entries of a collection whose
  elements are parts, stays with the document that stores that path. A read
  that covers a subtree with parts in it consumes the entries of every
  document the subtree is stored in.
- **A part's envelope is complete for its paths.** A part document has no
  label as a whole, apart from the root entry that holds the atom of the
  pattern, which every document of the keep set has (section 3.2). For each
  kept path inside it, its envelope holds every
  entry that a layout without the split holds for that path: the `value`
  entry with the instantiated template of that output path, with the
  element slots bound for the row's position, the frozen `shape` entry,
  and the declared entries. Where a `*`-child entry of a collection above
  the part covers the path, the part's envelope holds an entry at the path
  with that entry's label all the same. A read of a part document by its
  own address then consumes what a read of the same paths through the
  result consumes, and no path is served under a label that only another
  document holds.
- **The repeated entry and the `*`-child entry agree.** A `*`-child entry
  stays in the collection's document, where it covers the positions stored
  in place. It is written where every position instantiates to its label,
  the positions that are parts included, and one transaction writes it and
  the entries of the parts. Provisional (P31; "One entry for the elements
  of an array written whole" above): a position written later with another
  label adds an entry of its own and is read with the union, which is wider
  than its own label and never narrower. A read through the result that consumes
  both consumes one label twice, which a join absorbs. The entries of a
  part are those of the position its row has: a move that changes a label
  the row's slots resolve to rewrites them in the transaction that moves
  the row.
- **A storage link reveals no element key.** A storage link is part of what
  is stored, and a reader who may read the document that holds it can see
  it. For a row, that is a reader of the collection's membership. The
  identifier the link names must therefore tell that reader nothing of
  the element: an identifier derived from a cell's identity could be
  compared with one derived from a guessed cell. Provisional (P28 of the
  continuation plan): the identifier of a part that is a row or lies below
  a row is a number that the runtime mints and holds no key of an element,
  hashed or not (`execution-and-storage.md` §4.10). It then tells such a
  reader which entries hold the same part before and after a change of
  membership, which the membership label covers, and nothing of the cell
  or the value a row was computed from. Where the number is drawn from a
  counter it also tells the order in which parts were created, which that
  document lists as open. No client needs to derive the identifier: a
  reader names the result cell and a path.
- **One transaction writes them.** An evaluation writes the result document
  and every part document it changed in one transaction, so no reader sees
  a value in one document under a label from another state.
- **The checks are on result paths.** The constraints of section 4.4 are
  evaluated per output path and per write edge, and do not depend on which
  document stores the path.

**A link between scope instances.** A kept output of narrower scope than
the scope instance that holds its path is stored in the narrower scope
instance of the same document, and the broader one holds a link in its
place (`execution-and-storage.md` §4.2). That link is a storage link too.
It names the same document and path and holds the narrower declared scope,
with no user or session identifier, and nothing else: no schema and no
label entry. The properties above hold for it.

- The runtime writes it and no pattern code holds it. An `identity` slot
  does not observe it, it is not on a slot's chain, and it gives an
  element no cell identity as a key: a row whose kept value is of session
  scope is keyed as it would be if the value were stored in place.
- A read that passes through it consumes nothing for it. Every
  observation class at the path consumes the entries that the narrower
  scope instance's envelope holds for the path, which are the ones the
  output's template instantiated to for that scope key.
- The transaction that stores a value in a narrower scope instance writes
  the link in the same transaction.

The scope an output has at run time can be narrower than the plan's
(section 1.4), so whether a path of the broader scope instance holds a
value or such a link can depend on data. Section 5.5 lists it.

Whether a subtree is split off follows a rule about size, and size is a
function of data. An observer who can list the documents of a space can
see it, and so can a reader of the document that holds the storage link.
Section 5.5 lists this with the residuals.

### 2.4 Label metadata, and the inventory's three unplaced reads

`builtin-inventory.md` (open question 1) lists three reads that do not fit
value, shape, enumeration, or identity. Each is placed as follows.

- **Truthiness at the root of a condition** needs no new class. It is `value`
  at the root for a scalar and `shape` at the root for a record or array,
  whose truthiness is its existence (section 3.5).
- **The pointer label of a link that is followed** is the `identity` slot of
  the link. It resolves to the slot's `followRef` entries, and following the
  link joins it with the target's observations (section 3.10).
- **Label metadata** is a fifth class, `labelMetadata`. The specification
  makes observing a label a labeled observation of its own (§4.6.4.1,
  `04-label-representation.md`), and the runtime already has the class
  (`LABEL_METADATA_OBSERVATION` in
  `runtime/runner/src/cfc/label-view-core.ts`).

A `labelMetadata` slot does not read the value at its path. Its label is the
label of the metadata observation, which the runtime resolves from the
label-metadata templates of the target's envelope and computes in hand where
there are none
([label metadata confidentiality](../cfc-label-metadata-confidentiality.md)
§3). Where that label cannot be established the observation fails closed and
the read returns the constant the built-in defines for "not available". The
runtime records such an observation on the transaction today
(`recordCfcLabelMetadataObservation`, called from `inspectStoredConfLabel` in
`runtime/runner/src/cfc/label-introspection.ts`), and the flow join consumes
its confidentiality; the template's `slot` node does the same.

### 2.5 Paths that cross links, resolved references, and sampled reads

**A slot path may cross a link.** A slot's path is resolved from its root
the way a read resolves it. Where the value at a segment is a stored link,
resolution continues at the link's target. That is the case for an argument
path that holds a link to a cell of the parent, for a position of a data
type that storage holds as a link to a record's own document, and for a
path that continues below a cell handle. The addresses of the links crossed
are the slot's **chain**, and the address where resolution ends is where
the slot is **bound**.

- **Label.** The slot's confidentiality is the join of the `followRef`
  entries at each address of the chain with what the slot's class consumes
  at the bound address (section 2.2). Its integrity is that of the
  observation at the bound address alone: a pointer contributes
  confidentiality and no integrity
  ([CFC observation classes](../cfc-observation-classes.md) §6.1). This is
  what a journaled read through the same links consumes today, so the
  definition of section 2.2 already covers it, and §8.2.4
  (`08-02-pass-through-via-references.md`) requires it of a dereference.
  One case differs: a slot that reads as a default has the empty
  integrity ("A default belongs to the place", below).
- **`identity` stops at its last segment.** The chain of an `identity` slot
  holds the links crossed before the last segment, and the slot observes
  the reference stored there. Every other class resolves through a link at
  the last segment, with the one exception that follows.
- **A `shape` slot in place.** A `shape` slot with `inPlace` stops at its
  last segment too. It observes whether the position holds anything. A
  `shape` slot without the flag, at the same path, observes the root of the
  cell that a link at the position leads to. A body that writes
  `profile?.get()` on an optional handle makes both observations: the test
  of whether a handle is present is at the position, and the read is in
  the cell. Where the position holds a link, the slot in place resolves as
  a `followRef` read of the position, which is the read that hands a body
  the handle today. The label of which reference a position holds covers
  that it holds one. Where the position holds no link, the slot resolves
  as a `shape` read of the position.

  The flag is set on every `shape` slot at a position of handle type, and
  on every `shape` slot at a position of reference type, which is
  `unknown` in a data type (`language-subset.md` §7.8). A position typed
  `unknown` holds a reference whose target the code cannot read, so a test
  of presence or kind there is a test of the position, whatever is stored
  behind the reference. Without the flag the slot would resolve through
  the reference and take the label of the root of a cell that the code
  never observes.
- **A hop made by `key`.** `key` flattens every handle it passes through
  (`language-subset.md` §4.7): for `h` of type `Cell<{ a: Cell<T> }>`,
  `h.key("a")` is the handle at the position `a` of the cell `h` links
  to, written `h->a`. No `get()` makes the hop through `h`, and the path
  crosses the link all the same. The `identity` slot at `h->a` has the
  link of `h` on its chain and observes the reference stored at `a`, by
  the rule above. A slot below `h->a` has both links on its chain. The
  observation is made where the flattened handle is read, written
  through, passed on or bound (`footprint-analysis.md` §7.1).
- **Rebinding.** A change at an address of the chain changes where the slot
  is bound, and the slot's label is resolved again from the new chain. How
  a chain is watched belongs to `scheduler-and-serving-loop.md`.
- **Other instances and other spaces.** A chain can end in the result of
  another instance or in another space. The slot is a slot all the same,
  and its label is what a read at the bound address consumes there.
- **Storage links are not on a chain** (section 2.3).
- **A path that holds `*`.** A slot whose path has a `*` segment stands
  for every child the path reaches. It is bound at one address per child,
  and each of those bindings has a chain of its own: the links crossed on
  the way to that child, the link a position of the container holds
  included. The children are known once the container was read, so the
  bindings are made then, and a change of the container's children binds
  the slot again, as a change of membership binds element slots again
  (`scheduler-and-serving-loop.md` §3.2). The slot's confidentiality is
  the join, over the children, of what the rules above give each binding.
  Its integrity is the atoms that the observation at every one of the
  bound addresses carries. Which children there are is the membership of
  each container on the path. The slot's own label does not hold it: a
  footprint that has a slot below `*` has the `enumeration` slot of that
  container as well (`footprint-analysis.md` §3.1), and a template that
  joins the one joins the other. Where the runtime has verified by identity
  which child's reference a body passed on (section 3.9), the label of
  that reference is the label of that child's binding alone. This is what
  the journaled reads of the same children consume today.
- **A value that holds links.** A read of a value observes more than the
  bound address where the value holds links below it. A `value` slot
  consumes the subtree at its bound address (section 2.2), and a read of
  that subtree is made through every link it holds: a list whose elements
  are links to records, a record with a member that is a link, and a view
  whose children are links are read as the values those links lead to. The
  slot is therefore bound at each position such a link leads to as well,
  and at the positions reached through the links those values hold in
  turn. Each further binding has a chain of its own: the chain of the
  slot's own binding, then the address in the value where the link is
  stored, as a link crossed. The slot's confidentiality is the join, over
  its own binding and every further one, of what the rules above give each:
  the `followRef` entries along the chain with what the class consumes at
  the address where the chain ends. Its integrity is the atoms that the
  observation at the end of every one of the chains carries, as for a path
  that holds `*`. A chain never ends at an address that holds a link:
  where two links lead to one position, the second is a link crossed on
  the way to that position. A slot of class `shape` or `enumeration`
  consumes nothing below its bound address, so it has no further binding,
  and an `identity` slot stops at the link. The three cases of a list
  differ here. For an array of references and for the result of another
  per-element construct whose positions hold links, the `value` slot of
  the whole list has one further binding per element. For an array of
  plain values in place the elements are part of the subtree at the bound
  address and need none. A write record gives the further bindings as
  chains below the slot's own. This is what a journaled read of the same
  value through its links consumes today.
- **Further bindings whose labels are equal are reported once.** The label of a
  slot is the join over its chains, and chains whose positions hold equal labels
  add nothing to it. A write record therefore gives one chain for each set of
  further bindings whose positions have equal label identifiers (provisional,
  P31; section 4.2), so a read of an array of references whose elements have one
  label reports one further binding, at any length. A chain with a position that
  the transaction wrote has no identifier for that position and is kept. The
  identifier that is compared is that of the observation the binding makes at
  each position: a link followed for the positions on the way and the slot's
  class at the end. A read of the value at a position that holds a link does not
  consume the label of the link observed as a reference, so two links written by
  transactions that read different labeled data have one identifier for a read
  of their values and two as references. For a position that holds a link the
  comparison therefore takes the identifier of the slot's class together with
  that of the reference. The elements of a `fold` are grouped by the same
  identifiers. The prototype compares them so (`Instance.#labelKey` of
  `base/pattern-compiler/exec/executor.ts`, with `TransactionHooks.labelOf`
  given the class of the observation). The report is smaller, but forming it
  this way still visits every position, so over an array of references the work
  is linear in the elements. Section 4.7 removes that walk: a read that covers
  the members of a container is bound by the groups kept with the collection
  (adopted by ruling, being built; section 8, question 186). For an array of
  plain values in place there is no further binding to report, and for the
  result of another per-element construct whose positions hold links the rule is
  that of an array of references.
- **A value in place under a template of one reference slot.** A template that
  is one `slot` node of the class `identity`, directly or through the `output`
  and `shared` nodes it names, says that the written path holds a reference.
  Where the evaluation stores a value in place at that path and no link, the
  write stored what the slot's positions hold, and its label is that of a
  `value` read of them: the slot is bound in the class `value` for that write,
  with the further bindings of a value that holds links. It applies to the
  record of an output and to the record of a write edge. Two constructs store
  such a value: the result of a `reduce`, over an array of references, over an
  array of plain values in place and over the result of another per-element
  construct, and the array that a spread child copies. For a `reduce` over the
  result of another per-element construct, whose elements are at no stored
  position, the slot is bound to the positions that the upstream evaluations
  read. A position that holds a link or a stream keeps the class `identity`.
- **The label rule of a removal through a handle.** By ruling (2026-11-20) a
  removal through a handle (`remove`, `removeAll`, `removeByValue`) removes in
  place, as `footprint-analysis.md` §6.1 has it, and its label rule is derived
  from the CFC specification and not from today's implementation. The derivation
  follows, with the specification cited by section and chapter file. For an
  array of references it gives the ruling as worded. For an array of plain
  values in place the specification, read by its letter, puts what the removal's
  decision read on every position from the first removed one on, and three
  further rulings of 2026-11-20 say where it is stored instead, what a moved
  element keeps, and what a removal that finds nothing writes.
  - *The operations.* All three take a member, no index and no predicate.
    `remove` removes the first position that holds the member, and `removeAll`
    and `removeByValue` every such position. A position holds the member where
    its reference is the one the member names, or, for a copy of a plain value,
    where its value equals the member's.
  - *The decision.* Call D the join of what decided the removal: the reference
    to the list and the member, in the class `identity`; the inputs of the body
    that decided that the removal runs, which is its template; over an array of
    references, the identity of the reference at each compared position and no
    target; over an array of plain values in place, the value of each compared
    position and of the member, since a copy is compared by value. `remove`
    compares up to and including the first match, and the other two compare
    every position. Over an array of references D holds no clause of a kept
    element's content.
  - *What the specification gives.* A reference that is passed on keeps its own
    restrictions, the receiving position takes the control and selection
    restrictions of the write, and the target keeps its labels; a value passed
    on in place keeps its labels joined with those restrictions (section 8.2.1,
    `08-02-pass-through-via-references.md`). Moving a reference between
    positions is no observation of it (section 4.6.3,
    `04-label-representation.md`, "Runtime wiring reads are not observations").
    A collection has structural labels at its own path, the enumeration
    observations, and member labels at each child path, and for a member that is
    a reference the child `value` is the reference identity (section 8.5.6.1,
    `08-05-collection-transitions.md`). A static read of a position consumes
    nothing at the parent (section 4.6.3; section 8.9.5.1,
    `08-09-runtime-label-propagation.md`). The derived `value` and `iterate`
    entries are replaced by the committing transaction's derivation on an
    overwrite, the `shape` entry of a path is fixed at the path's creation, and
    the component carried by a link is replaced when the reference at the path
    is written again (section 8.12.8, `08-12-store-label-monotonicity.md`).
    Where the runtime's own writes determine a container's membership, or the
    positions receive references from the writing transaction, the runtime may
    mint entries at the container's wildcard child path from the join of the
    membership decision (section 4.6.3, "Wildcard per-class entries").
  - *The enumeration of the list, in every case.* The list after the removal has
    the members it had, less those D chose. Its enumeration label is the stored
    enumeration joined with D. It is a join and no replacement: which members
    remain is a function of which members there were. It is stored at the list's
    path in the `iterate` classes. The `shape` entry of the list's own path is
    not written, since the path still exists. The `shape` entries of the last
    positions, which no longer exist, are cleared, and what they held is in the
    stored enumeration.
  - *An array of references.* A kept element is a target document. The removal
    does not write it and does not observe it, and its label does not change.
    The reference at each position keeps the restrictions it carries, which move
    with it to the position it stands at. Which reference stands at a position,
    for every position from the first removed one on, is a selection of this
    transaction, with the label D. One entry at the list's `*` path can hold it,
    so no entry per kept element is written. A dereference through such a
    position consumes it. The removal writes the list's `iterate` entries, one
    selection entry at `*`, and the moved entries that the links carry. No
    target is labeled again. This is the ruling as worded.
  - *An array of plain values in place.* A kept element before the first removed
    position is not written, and its entries do not change. A kept element from
    the first removed position on stands at another position. A static read of a
    position consumes nothing of the list's enumeration, so D has to be consumed
    at the position: after `words.removeByValue(secret)` over `["a", "b"]`, a
    read of `words[0]` gives `"a"` or `"b"` by whether `secret` equals `"a"`.
    The element's own label is not joined with the labels of the other elements,
    except through D, where the comparison read them. Read by its letter the
    specification puts D on the `value` entry of every position from the first
    removed one on, since the value at that path changed. By ruling (2026-11-20)
    D is stored once for the list instead, as the next point has it.
  - *What decided a removal is stored once for the list.* By ruling (2026-11-20;
    Z71 of the continuation plan), after a removal from a list of plain values
    in place D is stored once for the list, as one entry at the list's `*` path
    in the `value` class, and a read of a position joins it with the position's
    own entry. The kept elements are therefore not labeled again, as the first
    ruling says, and a read of a position consumes D all the same. Successive
    removals join into the entry. A write that replaces the list clears it, and
    the label of that write then covers every member. The cost does not depend
    on the length of the list. What stays imprecise: a read of a member that
    stands before the first removed position consumes the entry too, although
    the removal did not change what that position holds.
  - *The specification sentence the rule needs,* as proposed, pending the
    specification pull request (section 8, question 191). Section 4.6.3 states
    the wildcard entries for a container whose slots hold references, and states
    the join of a wildcard entry with a concrete entry for the frozen `shape`
    entry alone ("Frozen existence joins with membership templates"). For the
    `value` class of a plain value in place a more specific entry replaces, so a
    member's own `value` entry would replace the entry at `*`. Proposed for the
    paragraph "Wildcard per-class entries (conforming template representation)",
    after the sentence that lists what the per-class twins cover:

    > The same holds where a writer changes the membership of a container of
    > values stored in place by removing members: the runtime MAY store the join
    > of what decided the removal once, as per-class twins at the container's
    > wildcard child path, in place of rewriting the `value` entry of every
    > member the removal moved. A wildcard twin minted this way is *additive* in
    > the `value` class as well: the effective `value` label of a child is the
    > join of the twin and the child's own most specific `value` entry, and a
    > more specific concrete entry does not replace the twin. Successive
    > membership decisions join into the twin; it is cleared only by a write
    > that replaces the container, whose own derivation then labels every
    > member.

    The sentence adds a second exception to the rule that a more specific entry
    replaces. It could be written as a fourth rule of the wildcard form, "A
    membership twin of the `value` class joins with a member's own entry".
  - *The result of another per-element construct.* The result of `map`, `filter`
    or `flatMap` is computed, and a body has no handle to remove through it. A
    removal from the source of such a construct is one of the two cases above
    for the source. The derived collection follows from its membership template:
    the elements that remain keep their keys, their state per key and their
    labels, no kept element is evaluated again for the removal, and the
    membership label is the template over the source's enumeration, which holds
    D. After a removal from the source, which element stands at a position of
    the derived collection depends on D as well. *Assumed, as built in milestone
    4 of the integration and not ruled* (section 8, question 192): where the
    members of a kept result of a per-element construct change otherwise than by
    an addition at its end, the label of the collection's membership, which
    holds D, is stored once for the positions of the result, as entries at its
    `*` path in the classes `value`, `shape` and `followRef`, in place of the
    ones the path carried, and a read of a position joins them with the
