    position's own entries (`PlanWrite.membersChanged` of
    `runtime/runner/src/cfc/types.ts`). It holds over an array of references,
    over an array of plain values in place and over the result of another
    per-element construct as the source. An addition to the source puts nothing
    on a position of the derived collection and leaves those entries as they are
    ("An addition through a handle" below).
  - *Entries stored per position, when positions shift.* The specification keys
    every entry by path and has no operation that moves the members of an array.
    By ruling (2026-11-20; Z72 of the continuation plan) a kept element that
    moves keeps its integrity: the runtime moves the stored label entries with
    the members of an array it splices, and no template is instantiated for the
    kept element. A template of the removal's write edge is a `derive`, which
    would take the integrity common to its inputs and mint the atom of the body,
    so an element labeled by it would lose its own integrity atoms. The `shape`
    entries do not move: a position that still exists keeps the entry of its
    creation, whichever element stands there. That is consistent because the
    stored enumeration holds every child's `shape`. The entries of a position
    that no longer exists after the removal are dropped, and a position created
    again mints its existence entry again (section 8.12.8).
  - *A removal that finds nothing* leaves the list as it was, and that it is
    unchanged reveals D. By ruling (2026-11-20; Z73 of the continuation plan) it
    is a label write of the enumeration, as a write that leaves a value as it
    was stores its label (section 3.12): the enumeration of the list takes D and
    no value is written.
  - *As built in milestone 4 of the integration.* The prototype's executor
    removes in place: each run of removed positions next to each other is one
    splice of the stored list, no kept member is written by the executor, and a
    kept reference stays the reference it was (`Handle.#removeAt` of
    `base/pattern-compiler/exec/executor.ts`). `Handle.#positionsOf` reports
    what the comparison read: which positions the list has; over an array of
    references the reference at each compared position, and nothing of the
    document it names; over an array of plain values in place the value at each
    compared position. The executor gives two write records for a removal,
    whatever the length of the list: one for the number of members and one for
    the membership of the list (`PlanWrite.enumeration` of
    `runtime/runner/src/cfc/types.ts`), which names the runs of members that
    moved (`PlanWrite.moves`, `PlanWrite.start`) and that members were removed
    (`PlanWrite.removes`). Both hold what the comparison read
    (`PlanWrite.decided`) and what the list stored of its membership
    (`PlanWrite.observed`). The runtime stores the label of the membership
    record as the `enumerate` entry at the list's path, for an array of plain
    values in place as for an array of references. It joins D into the list's
    `*`-child entries of origin `structure` in the classes `value`, `shape` and
    `followRef`, confidentiality alone; a member's own entries are of origin
    `derived`, and the resolution resolves each origin on its own and joins the
    results (`resolvedEntryGroups` of
    `runtime/runner/src/cfc/consumed-label.ts`), so the join of the ruling needs
    no change of the resolver. It carries the `derived` and `structure` entries
    of a moved member under the member's new path (`memberEntryPlacement` of
    `runtime/runner/src/cfc/prepare.ts`). A removal that finds no member gives
    the two records as those of writes that left the value as it was
    (`Instance.membersKept`). The `*` entries are kept for a list that a removal
    leaves empty. The deciding sites carry the `SPEC-PENDING` marker for specs
    pull request 91. One defect is open and not fixed (section 8, question 201):
    `resolvedEntryGroups` resolves the classes `value` and `followRef` of origin
    `structure` by the longest prefix, so a concrete `structure` entry further
    down, such as the entry that a recorded link write mints at a slot, replaces
    the `*` entry of a removal for that slot, and a read there does not consume
    what decided the removal. The fix resolves an entry that the runtime minted
    at a `*` path in a group of its own, as the `shape` class is resolved. It
    changes the resolution with the experimental option off, so it waits for the
    specification sentence above.
- **An addition through a handle.** For `push`, `pushAll` and `addUnique` the
  enumeration of the list after the addition is the stored enumeration joined
  with what decided the addition, by the same argument as for a removal. An
  added element is a member at its own position, with its own label, and the
  elements the list held are not written. The template of a `push` holds the
  reference to the list and the pushed value, and nothing of what the list
  stored, so the label of what the list held has to stay where it is stored. By
  ruling (2026-11-20; Z74 of the continuation plan) an append through a handle
  does not put the membership of the list, or what else the list holds, on the
  position it writes or on a position of a per-element result over the list: the
  operation appends a member whatever the list holds, and what the list holds
  does not decide whether it appends or where. As the coordinator of this work
  reads the ruling, which is not the owner's wording: the number of members and
  the enumeration still carry what decided each addition, and a read of a
  position by index consumes the position's own entry alone (section 4.6.3), so
  which member stands at an index after appends is an accepted channel. A
  removal is not affected, since its comparison decides which member stands at
  the later positions. A `push` under a condition that a labeled input decides
  needs no rule of its own: the write template of a handler joins every slot
  that its body reads statically (section 3.12), so every write of the handler
  carries the label of the condition. *Provisional (P39 of the continuation
  plan; the coordinator's decision, no owner ruling):* the list has an
  enumeration entry at its own path, replaced as above, and an added element is
  recorded at its own position, over an array of plain values in place and over
  an array of references. *As built in milestone 4 of the integration:* a splice
  of a stored array is written as the number of members and the positions it
  changed, so the entries of the positions before it stay. The executor gives
  one record for each added member at its position, one for the number of
  members and one for the membership (`Instance.#memberWrites`). The record of
  an added member holds the label of the write and of what the method compared,
  and nothing of what the list stored of its membership, as the ruling has it;
  the records of the number of members and of the membership hold it.
  `addUnique` compares as a removal does: where the list holds the member,
  nothing is added and the number of members and the membership take what the
  comparison read. A write through `key(n).set` at the position behind the last
  member is recorded as an addition. The plan has an envelope and no write edge
  for such a write, so its records have no inputs and are given as bound: each
  takes the transaction's join, joined for the number of members and the
  membership with what the list stored of them (`PlanWrite.bound`). A write that
  replaces an array stores its label as the `enumerate` entry of the array as
  well. Three further rules close reads that consumed nothing of what decided
  the members, each behind the experimental option:
  - *A read of a position that holds no member consumes the list's membership.*
    That a position holds no member says how many members the list has. For a
    content read at a path through such a position, the resolver joins what a
    read of the list's membership consumes: the `enumerate` entry at the list's
    path and the entries above it
    (`ObservationLabelResolver.#membershipOfAbsent` of
    `runtime/runner/src/cfc/observation-label.ts`). It holds for an array of
    plain values in place and for an array of references. It is the first
    alternative of section 8, question 193.
  - *An array inside a value written whole takes the label of the write as its
    `enumerate` entry.* The entry is stored at the path of each array that the
    written value holds, the target of a reference excepted, and takes the label
    of the nearest path above the array that stores a label in the commit. It is
    the first alternative of section 8, question 194, and is linear in the
    arrays written.
  - *A write that leaves a path holding nothing stores its label at the path.*
    After `key(i).set(undefined)` the position holds nothing, and a reader of it
    consumes what decided the write.

  What the ruling on an append leaves open: a member appended after a removal.
  For a stored list the `*` entries of the removal are joined on a read of the
  later position. Whether every such position of a kept per-element result
  stores a clause of what decided the earlier removal is not established
  (section 8, question 192).

A read stays `dynamic` where the plan cannot name its path ahead of the
evaluation: a read through a handle that happens on some runs only or at a
path the body computes (section 3.9), and a read through a reference the
instance computed (section 3.10).

**A resolved reference.** An `identity` slot with `resolved` observes the
reference where resolution ends: the links are followed from the slot's
path until a cell is reached whose value is not a link. Its chain includes
those further links, and its label joins the `followRef` entries at each.
The reference the runtime hands to code for such a slot is the resolved
one. `resolveAsCell()` at a static place, `spaceOf`, and the other calls
section 3.16 lists observe a reference this way.

**A sampled read.** A slot with `sampled` is a read made with `sample()`.
Its label joins the template like any slot's. A change at its address,
of the value or of the label, does not make a cone stale and gives no
output a new instantiation key: the label that enters the key is the one
resolved when the cone was last evaluated. A `sample()` through a handle
of `Body.handles` is journaled and joins the `dynamic` label in the same
way, and is not registered as something that makes the cone stale. Today a
sampled read is made through a transaction that journals it and marks it
as not scheduling (`sample` in `runtime/runner/src/cell.ts`), so the label
is **equal**.

**A default belongs to the place.** By ruling, a default belongs to the
stored place, and a reader bound to the place by reference gets a link and
not a copy. A link holds, beside the address it names, the schema of the
place it names, as the plan of the instance that wrote the link declares
it, and so the default that declaration has. A slot whose path crosses a
link is read under the schema of the slot, with one member taken from the
chain: the default of the link nearest the bound address whose schema
declares one. Where no link of the chain declares one, the default of the
slot's own schema applies. Everything else the read validates against is
the slot's schema alone. So where nothing is stored at the bound address,
the slot reads as the default of the place's declaration, for every
reader, a reader whose own schema declares no default included.

By ruling that order is the rule: the default read at a position is the
one declared nearest the end of the chain of places the read resolves
through, the stored place last, and the reader's own default, a
callee's included, is read only where no place along the chain declares
one. The runtime of today reads the same for a read addressed at a
position. While it follows the chain it keeps the top-level `default` of
the last link schema that declares one (`resolveLink` in
`runtime/runner/src/link-resolution.ts`, with its helpers
`declaredDefault` and `withDefault`), and where it combines the reader's
schema with a link's, the link's default replaces the reader's
(`combineSchemaForLink` in `runtime/runner/src/traverse.ts`). A schema
on the handle through which the final document was written counts for
nothing in either, because it is not stored. For patterns that gives:
a caller's argument at which nothing is stored, or a bound cell, whose
declaration has a default wins over the callee's default, and the
callee's default is read where no place along the chain declares one.

- **A path that resolves without a stored link.** A path of the state of
  a binding of the reactive tier resolves to a slot of the instance
  (section 3.14), and a slot of a pattern compiled into another is an
  entry of the enclosing plan (section 1.1). No link is stored for
  either. The rule is the same: the read is made under the reader's
  schema with the default of the schema of the slot it resolves to
  (`Slot.schema`), which is the place's declaration. For a pattern
  compiled into another, by ruling, a path that the call binds to a
  slot at which nothing is stored also reads the default the callee
  declares for the path, and only where the place of the slot declares
  none, by the order above (section 1.1, "A constant of the argument,
  and a path the call leaves out"). By ruling a reference to such a
  path that the callee stores is a link that carries the callee's
  declared default, so the callee's declaration is on the chain of
  whoever reads through the link, before the caller's place.
- **A property default, in a read of an object whole.** The ruling
  speaks of the default read at a position. A slot that reads a stored
  object whole also reads the properties below its position, and a
  schema along the chain can declare a default for one of them. For
  such a read the runtime of today takes the top-level default of a
  link's schema alone: a default that the link's object schema declares
  for a property is dropped, and the reader's own default for the
  property is read. A selection of the same property, which is
  addressed at the property's position, reads the link's default.
  *Assumed* (section 8, question 103): the order above holds at every
  path of what a slot reads. A property that is absent reads the default
  that the place nearest the end of the chain declares for it, and the
  default of the slot's own schema where no place declares one, in a
  whole read as in a selection. That differs from today for the whole
  read, in the value alone: the integrity is that of the stored object
  either way ("The integrity", below).
- **A stored `undefined`, and a default written at setup.** In the
  runtime of today a stored `undefined` reads as an absent value does,
  so the default is read. A pattern of today also writes the defaults
  of its own argument schema into its argument document at setup, for
  each key that is absent (`#applySetupState` in
  `runtime/runner/src/runner.ts`), and such a default is from then on a
  stored value for whatever reads through the document. A key that
  holds a stored `undefined` is present, so nothing is written for it,
  and a read of it still gives the callee's default. *Assumed* (section
  8, question 104): in the compiled path a stored `undefined` reads as
  absent does, and the default the order above names is read. And no
  default is written into an argument document: a pattern compiled into
  another has no argument document, and for a `Child` the write edges
  of its argument write what the caller gave and nothing for a path the
  caller left out. A default is then always read and never stored, so
  it has the integrity of a default, and a default of a place nearer
  the end of the chain is not hidden by a stored copy of the callee's.
- **A state cell.** A first value that is a constant is the default of
  the cell's schema (section 1.3). A slot of root `state` that finds
  nothing stored reads it, by this rule, with the integrity below.
- **Which plan holds the default.** The reader's plan does not hold it.
  A handler is one `Body` however many bindings name it, and its
  `binding` slots have the schema its own state type declares. The
  default reaches a read at run time, from the link or from the slot the
  path resolves to. No record changes.
- **The confidentiality.** A default read through a link has the
  confidentiality of the slot, by the rules above and no further rule:
  the join of the `followRef` entries at each address of the chain with
  what the slot's class consumes at the bound address, where the read
  found nothing stored. This is the case of section 5.2 in which a slot
  reads as the default its schema declares, and the confidentiality is
  that of the slot there too. The link that holds the default is on the
  chain, so the label of which link the reader holds, and with it of
  which default, is joined. The default is a constant of the source of
  the pattern that declares the place. It does not enter the reader's
  templates as a `const`, because the reader's plan does not hold it: it
  is what the slot read.
- **The integrity.** By ruling, a read of a default carries no integrity, and
  integrity is anchored in a stored object as a whole. The first rule holds for
  a default of each of the three origins: the place's declaration, the schema of
  a link of the chain, and the slot's own schema (section 5.2).

  - **Nothing is stored at the bound address.** The slot has the empty
    integrity.

  - **A read of a stored object whole.** A slot bound at the address of a stored
    object carries the integrity of the observation at that address, also where
    a property of the object is absent and a default fills it. The claims were
    made about the object that is stored, and the slot reads that object. A
    default among its properties removes none of them.

  - **A selection of one property.** A path that selects a property is a slot of
    its own, bound at the property's address (sections 2.1 and 3.3), and it
    carries what a read at that address consumes (section 2.2). For each origin
    of entry that is the entry stored at the property's path, and, where none is
    stored there, the nearest entry above it that applies below its own path
    (`labelForEntriesAtPath` in `runtime/runner/src/cfc/consumed-label.ts`). So
    a selected property that is stored carries its own integrity where an entry
    is stored for it, and the integrity of the object's entry where the object's
    is the nearest. A selected property that is absent and that a default fills
    carries the empty integrity, by the first rule: the object's claims are
    about what is stored in it, and the selected value is not stored.

  The value of a default is not stored at the bound address, and no
  principal wrote it there. It comes from a schema, and a pointer
  contributes no integrity. An empty integrity under-claims, which is
  the fail-safe direction (§8.9 of `08-09-runtime-label-propagation.md`).
  The specification has no rule for a default that is read and not
  stored, and needs this one. Its §8.15 (`08-15-write-authority.md`)
  separates initialization from attribution and mints no principal claim
  for a default, and its §3.7.2 (`03-core-concepts.md`) gives a link no
  integrity that was not minted for it; neither says what integrity a
  reader finds where a schema supplied the value. A rule that requires
  integrity of a value therefore refuses a default, and a place that has
  to satisfy such a rule holds a stored value.
- **A write.** A write through a handle to such a place stores a value at
  the place, under the label of the writing edge. Every reader then reads
  that value, and the default is no longer read.
- **A copy is not a link.** Where a binding made in a function body
  copies a scalar (section 3.14), the copy holds what the body read. A
  scalar read from a place where nothing is stored, and whose declaration
  has a default, is copied as the default, with `T_b`.

Today a read that crosses a link continues under the reader's schema and
takes the default of the last link crossed whose schema declares one,
the reader's own where none does (`combineSchemaForLink` in
`runtime/runner/src/traverse.ts`; a payload of a link has a `schema`
member, `CellLinkRefPayload` in `runtime/runner/src/sigil-types.ts`). An
absent value takes the default of that combined schema before it is
validated (`materializeSchemaView` in `runtime/runner/src/schema-view.ts`,
through `defaultForAbsentValue`), and the read of the path found empty is
registered in the transaction, so the default carries the join that the
read contributes. A binding a pattern makes is written as a link with the
schema of the path it names (`unwrapOneLevelAndBindToDoc` in
`runtime/runner/src/pattern-binding.ts`). The value and the confidentiality are
**equal**. The integrity of a slot that reads a stored object whole is
**equal**. The integrity of a slot that reads as a default is **looser**: today
the read has the integrity of the entries that resolve at the bound address, an
entry of an enclosing object included, and by the rule above it has none. Fewer
integrity atoms is looser by the definition of section 3.1. The difference is
accepted by ruling, and section 3.1 lists it as the third exception.

**A handle to a position that holds nothing.** An `identity` slot at a
position of handle type yields a handle whether or not anything is stored
at the position. Where the position holds a link, the handle names the
cell the link leads to. Where it holds a plain value or nothing, the
handle names the position itself: that path of the document the slot's
root is in. So the body of a pattern is handed a handle for an optional
property of its input that the caller left out, and the handle names that
path of the instance's argument document. A read through it finds nothing
stored and gives the default of the declaration, by the rule above, or
what section 5.2 gives where there is none. A write through it lands at
that path. Whether such a position holds anything is observed by a `shape`
slot in place (above), and the `identity` slot's own label is that of the
`followRef` read of the position. Today a position declared as a cell is
handed to the body as a handle where nothing is stored
(`processDefaultValue` in `runtime/runner/src/schema.ts`, and the branch
for a link to an absent value of `#traversePointerWithSchema` in
`runtime/runner/src/traverse.ts`). **Equal.**

### 2.6 Stored state that is not an output

Beside outputs and write targets, the runtime stores state of its own: the
state of a durable operation, the entries of a cache, a provenance record
per kept output, the origin facts of a kept derived collection, the
record of the instances a computation made, and the rows a serving
runtime's scheduler keeps beside the documents of a space. Each is
derived from data, so each has a label. No template has a slot for any
of it except an operation's result, so these labels never join the label
of an output. They govern a reader that reaches the stored state by
another route, and what the runtime may show of it in a diagnostic or to a
tool.

| What is stored | Label |
| --- | --- |
| The result of an operation, a bucket of an index, a checkpoint of a `reduce` | The rule of the operation (sections 3.8, 3.11, 3.13, 3.17); for an effect, the declared rule of its boundary |
| Every other path of an operation's state document: a contribution per element key, an index key per element key, a count, and the request hash, the claim and the pending mark of an effect | The confidentiality of `Operation.input`, instantiated, and no integrity. For an effect it is joined with what following the references of the request consumed (section 3.14). An effect a handler requested has no `Operation` record, and the join is over the templates of the `request` write edges of its site |
| A cached output, of a cone the runtime promoted or of a forced cache | The output's own template, instantiated as for a kept output |
| Every other member of a cache entry: selections, the keys a `pick` chose, and what the entry records of the cone's reads | The confidentiality of the cone-level join (section 7.2), and no integrity |
| The provenance record of a kept output path: its selections, its instantiation key, the addresses of its dynamic reads | The confidentiality of the output's instantiated label, joined with the label of the label-metadata observation at the path, and no integrity |
| The origin facts of a kept derived collection | The collection's instantiated membership label |
| The record of which instances the last evaluation of a `lift` or a `computed` made at each site (section 3.14) | The confidentiality of the body's template, instantiated, and no integrity |
| The record of the children an element body has under an element key (`execution-and-storage.md` §2.5) | The collection's instantiated membership label, for each collection whose element key the record is stored under, and no integrity |
| The allocation record of a space an `inSpace` request creates (section 3.14) | The confidentiality of the requesting body's template, instantiated as section 3.14 says for a record that commits ahead of its unit, and no integrity |
| A path of any of these that holds label identifiers, such as the count per identifier a `fold` keeps (section 4.3) | The label of its row above, joined with the label of the label-metadata observation of each label it names |

Why each label covers what is stored:

- **Bookkeeping of an operation.** Every contribution is a function of the
  elements the operation folds, and `Operation.input` joins all of them and
  the membership. The label is wider than one contribution needs. Nothing
  the language has reads a contribution, so the width costs nothing.
- **The request hash of an effect.** `Operation.input` joins the templates
  of the request, and a path of the request that holds a reference has the
  label of the pointer. The hash is computed from the content behind those
  references, the operands that are hashed and not sent included. Its
  label is therefore the joined label of section 3.14, and the claim and
  the pending mark, which say that a request with that hash is being made,
  take the same label.
- **No integrity.** Bookkeeping is the runtime's own data structure and not
  a value an upstream claim describes, and the code named by a
  `TransformedBy` atom did not compute it. An empty integrity under-claims,
  which is the fail-safe direction (§8.9.3).
- **A cached output** is the value a kept output would be, so it has that
  label. A cache entry's other members are functions of what the cone
  read, which the cone-level join bounds.
- **A provenance record.** A selection is a function of the value of a
  condition, the instantiation key is a function of selections and labels,
  and an address a body read is a function of the body's inputs. The
  output's template joins the conditions and the body's footprint, and the
  label-metadata observation covers the labels. The label of the path's
  label metadata alone would not cover a selection.
- **Origin facts** say which elements a predicate admitted, or how long
  each segment was, which is what the derived collection's membership
  template joins (section 3.7).
- **The instances a computation made.** How many instances an evaluation
  makes at a site, and under which causes, is a function of what the body
  read, which the body's template joins.
- **The children of an element body.** A child that a factory value
  called in the reactive tier of an element body makes is no instance a
  computation made, and no body's template covers it. The runtime lists
  it all the same, per element key, in the instances document of the
  enclosing instance, so that a child whose key no position holds any
  more is found and torn down after a restart. The record says that the
  collection has an element with that key, which is what the membership
  label covers. Which child the record names follows from the key and
  the `Child` record, and adds nothing.
- **An allocation record.** That a space exists under a name, or for a
  request, is a function of what the requesting body read, and so is a
  name the body computed. The identifier the record holds is obtained and
  is a function of no data.

**Stores the runtime owns.** An operation's state document and a cache
document are written by the runtime alone, and no authored schema declares
a label for them. They are stores the runtime owns, in the sense in which
it owns a built-in's store today (`RuntimeOwnedStores` in
`runtime/runner/src/cfc/runtime-owned-stores.ts`): writer-fit has no
declared confidentiality to test a write against, no writer policy applies,
and what is stored is the derived label of the table above.

**Rows beside the documents.** The scheduler of a serving runtime keeps
three kinds of row in the space's store, beside the documents
(`scheduler-and-serving-loop.md` §10.4, §5.1 and §10.6): a basis row per
cone, scope instance and input document, which holds the sequence number
of that input at the last evaluation; a row of the stream index per
stream, which leads from the stream's identifier to its instance and its
binding; and a pending-effect row per effect operation that a handler
requested and that has a pending mark, which holds the operation's
state document, the result cell of the instance whose handler requested
it, and the requester, the principal the event was stamped with. The stream
index is ruled: an event is routed
through it to an instance that is not loaded. Its row takes the place of
the `result` back-link that setup stores on a stream's document today. A
row is not a document. It has no address a reference can name, no
envelope, and no stored label. That scheduler alone reads it: a row is
never sent to a client, never read at admission, and no pattern code
reaches it. A row is derived from data all the same. *Assumed:* where the
runtime shows one in a diagnostic or to a tool, it shows it under the
label below.

- **A row of the stream index** says that a stream exists. For a binding
  of the reactive tier in an element body it says that the collection has
  the element, so the row carries the collection's instantiated membership
  label, for each collection whose element key it holds. An element key
  derived from a value is held salted (section 1.3). For a binding made
  in a function body the row carries the identity label of the stream
  (section 3.14).
- **A pending-effect row** is written with the pending mark of the
  operation and deleted with it, and activation reads the rows to find
  the requests to make again. It says what the pending mark says, that a
  request of that operation is being made, so it carries the label of
  the pending mark: the joined label of section 3.14. The requester is
  the acting principal of the event, which the runtime attests and which
  carries no confidentiality (section 3.16), so it adds nothing to that
  label. The operation's
  state document holds a back-link to the same instance
  (`execution-and-storage.md` §6.4). The runtime writes that back-link
  and no pattern can write it, and which instance it names follows from
  the stream the event was sent to. Reading it joins no label, as reading
  the `result` back-link of a document joins none (section 3.16).
- **A basis row** says which documents a cone read, for one scope
  instance. For the reads
  of a `dynamic` node that is data, so the row carries the confidentiality
  of the cone-level join (section 7.2), as what a cache entry records of
  the cone's reads does. The scheduler also consults basis rows to decide
  whether a read returns a stored value without loading the instance that
  wrote it (section 5.4). That use shows no row to anyone and changes no
  label: the read joins the label stored at the address, as any read of a
  stored value does.

**The state of an operation inside an element body.** An `Operation` with
an `element` step in `within` has state per element key (section 1.3): an
aggregate declared in a row has one state per row. Whether that is one
document per key, or one document per operation with the state of each key
at a path of its own, changes no label. `execution-and-storage.md` chooses
one state document per key (its §6). The cause is the same in both: the
element key is a part of the identifier in the first layout and a path
segment in the second. Two things hold in either, and they hold for
everything else an element cone stores per key.

- **Each key's state has its own entries.** The state of one key is labeled
  by the table above, instantiated for that element, and in a document
  that holds several keys the entries are at that key's paths. The key set
  of such a document says which elements the collection has, so it carries
  the collection's instantiated membership label. A key derived from a
  value is the salted one in every layout (section 1.3). Two documents
  hold several element keys: the cache document, with one entry per
  element key of a promoted element cone, and the instances document,
  with one record per element key of an element cone that makes
  instances, and one per element key under which an element body has
  children (`execution-and-storage.md` §8.4, §2.8 and §2.5). In each,
  the set of keys under one cone carries that membership label. Under a
  nested element body the keys of the inner collection carry the inner
  collection's membership label, instantiated for the outer element.
- **What is stored per key carries the label of one position.** A key
  stands at one position of its collection (section 1.3), and the element
  slots of the key resolve at that position. Everything an element cone
  stores is stored per key (`execution-and-storage.md` §2.5): a kept
  output, the state of an operation, the stored request and the result of
  an effect, a path of the argument of a child or of an instance the cone
  makes, a side-write, a copied path of a binding or of an inline
  pattern's parameters, an entry of the cache document, and the record in
  the instances document. Each is labeled by its own rule, instantiated
  for that key. Nothing is stored once for several positions of a
  collection, so no stored label joins the labels of two positions, and
  the rule that labels flow per value through the callback of a
  per-element construct (section 3.6) holds at every position: two
  positions that hold equal plain values, or links to one cell, under
  different labels have two keys, and what is stored for each carries
  the label of its own position alone. In the runtime of today each
  occurrence of an element has an element run of its own (`listElementKeys`
  in `runtime/runner/src/builtins/list-element-keys.ts` adds an
  occurrence count to the key), so the rule is equal to today there.

  A stream of a binding of the reactive tier in an element body is per
  key as well (section 1.3), and an event on it names one key. When an
  event arrives, each element slot of the handler's state resolves at
  the position that holds the key. A handler that closes over the
  element alone therefore writes under the event and that element, and
  under nothing of an equal element at another position.

**A stored link that becomes a value.** When an instance stored by the
current runtime is first written in the compiled layout, a result path that
held a link to a node's document comes to hold the value
(`execution-and-storage.md`, section 9). The write is an overwrite of an
existing path. Its `value` entry is replaced by the instantiated template,
as on any overwrite. Its frozen `shape` entry is kept (§8.12.8,
`08-12-store-label-monotonicity.md`) and is joined with the confidentiality
of the `followRef` entries the link had: that the path exists was decided
by the write of that link, and a reader of the value consumes the `shape`
entry where it used to consume the pointer's. The stored label of the path
is then never looser after the migration than before it.

## 3. Label rules of the structural operations

Each rule gives the template the compiler emits, the confidentiality and
integrity it instantiates to, and how that compares with what the runtime
computes today.

### 3.1 The baseline: what the runtime computes today

Today a reactive node run is one transaction, and every path the transaction
writes gets one label:

- `deriveFlowJoin` (`deriveFlowJoinImpl` in
  `runtime/runner/src/cfc/prepare.ts`) computes one join per transaction over
  the reads `forEachFlowObservation` yields, and
  `prepareBoundaryCommitSteps` stamps it on every written path. The kernel
  manifest states it in its `propagateLabels` row
  (`runtime/runner/src/cfc/kernel/manifest.ts`).
- Confidentiality is the union of what every counted read consumed, trigger
  reads included
  ([CFC observation classes](../cfc-observation-classes.md) §6).
- Integrity is the hereditary meet over the content observations, plus a
  `TransformedBy` atom minted by `mintTransformedBy`
  (`runtime/runner/src/cfc/input-witness.ts`) when every write of the
  transaction was made under one known implementation identity and the join
  has a confidentiality clause or a hereditary atom (`deriveFlowJoinImpl`).
  Beside that atom, which holds the identity alone, `mintTransformedBy`
  mints one atom that holds the identity and an `inputWitness` for each
  `TransformedBy` atom that every confidential location the transaction
  read carries (`retainedInputWitnesses` and `meetInputWitnesses` in the
  same file; [input witnesses](../cfc-transformed-by-input-witnesses.md)).
  The [conformance statement](../cfc-conformance-statement.md) §4 records
  this as the third stage of §8.9.3 with deviations.
- Input gates (`verifyInputRequirements`) quantify over the reads before the
  last overlapping write
  ([write-prefix provenance](../cfc-write-prefix-provenance.md)); the join
  itself stays transaction-global
  ([value-level provenance](../cfc-value-level-provenance.md) §1).
- **A static part, from declarations.** Beside the join of a run, the result of
  a node carries the confidentiality that its inputs declare.
  `createNodeFactory` (`runtime/runner/src/builder/module.ts`) joins the
  confidentiality a module's argument schema declares onto the module's result
  schema (`applyArgumentIfcToResult` in
  `runtime/runner/src/builder/node-utils.ts`), and `connectInputAndOutputs` in
  that file joins the confidentiality that the schemas of a node's input cells
  declare onto the schemas of its outputs (`applyInputIfcToOutput`). The result
  document holds that join as an entry of origin `declared`, beside the
  `derived` entry of the transaction's join where the run stores one (for
  `ifElse` it stores none where the selected branch is a reference, section
  3.5). It is fixed when the graph is built and does not depend on what a run
  read. It applies to every node: a `lift`, a
  `computed`, `ifElse`, and the result of `map`
  (`runtime/runner/test/cfc-argument-ifc-propagation.test.ts` states it for a
  module). So the result of `ifElse` carries the declared confidentiality of the
  condition and of both branches whichever branch is selected, and the container
  of a `map` result carries the confidentiality its elements declare.

So today the label of a written path is a function of *which transaction wrote
it*, joined with that static part, and precision comes from giving each node its
own transaction. In the comparisons below, "today" means that per-node
arrangement.

**The static part is not copied.** By ruling, a template does not join the
labels that the arguments of an operation declare. `ifElse` and the container of
a `map` are trusted in exactly this sense: their result does not join the labels
of all their arguments. The static part is recorded as a finding against the
runtime, which is wider there than its own `derived` entry, and the design does
not reproduce it. A template is therefore **tighter** than today wherever the
static part holds a clause that the template lacks. For a conditional and for
the container of a `map` that is the one difference from today (sections 3.5 and
3.6). For every other rule the comparison words of this section describe the
template against the `derived` part, and the static part can narrow a template
further without a rule saying so.

**What is compared.** The two sides do not store the same thing at an output
path. Today a result path holds a link to a document of the node that computed
it, and a node that returns an input stores a copy of its value. A template for
a value passed on is the `identity` slot of the input, and the plan stores a
reference. *Assumed* (section 8, question 65): the comparison is made on
dereferenced labels. For the runtime that is what a value read of the output
path consumes with every link followed (`cfcLabelViewForResolvedCell` in
`runtime/runner/src/cfc/label-view.ts`). For the template it is the label of
section 3.2, with each `identity` slot that stands for the reference the
output passes on joined with what a value read at the slot's path consumes:
the `slot` node that is the output's template, or one that is the selected
branch of a `select` or the `body` of a `pick`, which is the template of
the chosen child. An `identity` slot at any other place of a template is
not dereferenced: an input of a `derive`, the `condition` of a `select`,
the `choice` of a `pick`, and a slot in the `body` of a `fold`. It has the
label of section 2.2, the label of the link, because the code that holds
the handle did not read through it, and by ruling the label of the
handle's cell is not in what that code writes. Where the handle is only
passed on, that label leaves out the `link` entry of the position, which
repeats the label the cell's type declares, and where the slot is
`resolved` it holds that entry (section 2.2). For an entry
that names a collection, the runtime's side
is what a read of the container's shape consumes. The runtime's entries are
separated by origin: the `derived` entries are compared with the template, and a
difference that the `declared` entries of the static part account for is
expected. Sixteen more rules fix what a row of the comparison is.

- **A constructed container.** An output entry that has entries below it is
  compared as an entry that names a collection is: the runtime's side is what
  a read of the container's shape consumes. A value read of the container
  consumes the labels of everything below it, and the template of the
  container entry does not hold them (section 3.4).
- **Integrity is a set of atoms.** An atom is compared by the canonical form
  of the whole atom, and it counts once however many entries of a label view
  hold it. Where a read covers several stored paths, the runtime's side has
  the atoms that every one of them holds, which is what a read of the whole
  has.
- **An atom that names code.** The runtime's `TransformedBy` atom for the
  callback of a promoted `computed` and the template's atom for the pattern
  that contains it name different code (section 3.2). The comparison takes
  the two as corresponding: a row is equal on them where each side has its
  atom, and no row is looser because the identities differ.
- **The atom of an output that passes a value on by reference.** By ruling
  (2026-11-20) the pattern's atom is in the label of the content at the output
  path, with no scope, and a read through the link takes it (section 3.2). The
  template's side of the row holds that atom beside the integrity of the
  dereferenced value, as the runtime's side, a copy the callback wrote, holds
  its atom in one label with the value.
- **A selection the harness cannot establish.** `sel(i)` of section 3.2 is
  what the value code reports. A harness that has no value code reads the
  selection from the stored values, and a row whose selection it cannot
  establish that way is a bound over the branches and is counted apart. It is
  not a row of the comparison.
- **The atom of a kept output.** Every kept output carries the atom of its
  pattern (section 3.2), and the runtime stores no atom for a value that a
  pattern passes on or for a value with no label. With the atom, such a row
  is tighter on integrity whatever its template is, so the atom would hide
  what the rule of the template does. Each row is therefore classified
  twice: on the template's label without the atom of the kept output, and
  on the label with it. The first classification is the test of the rule
  the row's template follows (section 3.22). The second is the label the
  design stores. A row of the third exception below has, with the atom,
  the pattern's atom and not the atoms of the stored object, so neither
  integrity holds the other. It is counted as that exception by its first
  classification, and not as a row that cannot be compared.
  By ruling every commit of a compiled pattern is prepared (section 3.2,
  "Every commit is prepared"), so a row whose template's label without the
  atom is empty still has the atom on the stored side.
- **A value at a child position that is the result of a pattern.** The plan
  has the entries of the callee's `[UI]` at the position (section 1.1). The
  runtime holds the callee's result there, with its tree under `$UI`. A row
  at a path at or below the position is read from the runtime at the same
  path below `$UI` of that result.
- **A reference whose target no slot names.** The template of an output can
  be the label of a reference that the instance computed: a handle that a
  site of a body made (section 3.9, "A reference a site of the body made"),
  or any other `identity` entry of `Body.computed`. The plan names no
  address for the target. The template's side is joined with what a value
  read through the link stored at the runtime's output path consumes, the
  entries of the target's own document included. Both sides then read one
  target, and the row compares the labels of the reference. A body can
  also return a value it computed with such a reference inside it, such as
  a tree that an authored function builds with the handle at an attribute
  of one of its elements. The output's template is then the body's
  `derive`, and the reference is at a path below the output path that the
  plan does not name. The template's side is joined with what a value read
  through each link stored below the output path consumes. The row is
  exact where the reference is the one link stored there. Where the run
  stored another link below the path it is a bound, because a stored link
  does not say which site made it. For a slot of
  root `operation` that holds what a materializer returned (section 3.11),
  the runtime's counterpart is the result document of the node that ran
  the body.
- **An output the run holds no value at.** It is not a row of the
  comparison, and it is counted apart by its reason. A position the run did
  not render, below a conditional that selected another branch or beyond
  the end of an array, and a link to a cell that holds no value, store
  nothing on either side. An output of a computation that threw stores
  nothing in the runtime, which commits none of the writes of a node that
  throws, so the runtime has no label there. The compiled path stores an
  error state under the output's template (section 5.2), by the ruling
  that a failed cone takes a labeled error state. *Assumed* (section 8,
  question 76): the template's clauses at such an output are not counted
  as looser than today, and the output is no further exception.
- **A write edge of a handler.** A write edge is a row where the scenario sent
  the handler an event, the event's transaction committed, and the run wrote the
  edge's target. The runtime's side is what a value read of the written path
  consumes after the event, with every link followed, as for an output. The
  template's side is the edge's template, beside the label that the target's own
  type declares for the written path, which is stored there on both sides
  (section 3.12). In the template each slot of root `event` has the label the
  event arrived with (section 3.12), each slot of root `binding` resolves
  through the binding the event was sent to, and each `identity` slot among the
  inputs of the body's `derive` has the label of the link and is not
  dereferenced (section 2.2). For a handle that the body neither reads nor
  writes through, and whose slot is not `resolved`, that label leaves out the
  `link` entry of the position. Only an edge with a `reference` member, whose
  written value is the reference, is joined with what a value read through the
  stored link consumes, so that both sides read one target. The integrity of
  such a row is that of the value read through the link, on both sides. What is
  stored at the written path is a link, and a read through a link takes its
  integrity from the target alone (section 3.10). The atom that the edge's
  template mints for the body is in the label of the link, and the row counts
  neither it nor the integrity of the `followRef` entry that the runtime stamped
  at the link. The ruling that puts the atom of a kept output on the content
  (section 3.2) names kept outputs, and a write edge is *assumed* unchanged by
  it (section 8, question 72). An event whose transaction did not commit gives
  no row, and neither does a write that the run did not make. A run makes no
  write where the handler returns before it or takes another branch on the event
  it was sent, and where the value it writes equals what the target holds,
  because a write changes only the paths whose value differs (`diffAndUpdate` in
  `runtime/runner/src/data-updating.ts`). A scenario therefore gives the members
  of an event values that its inputs do not hold, and an event whose declared
  type is a scalar is a value of that type. The outcome is read from the event's
  transaction and not from a log: the runtime reports it once per event
  (`sendEvent` in `runtime/runner/src/cell.ts`, with a callback that
  `runFinalCommitCallback` and `notifyEventDropped` in
  `runtime/runner/src/scheduler/events.ts` call), and a handler that threw logs
  no refusal. Such events are counted apart by their reason. A scenario has to
  give its inputs labels under which the events commit: writer-fit measures what
  a handler read against the ceiling of each store it writes (section 4.4), so a
  generated clause on an input has to be one that every store of the scenario's
  space admits, and an input is stored under the schema the runtime's argument
  schema has for it (section 8, question 80). A member of an event that is
  declared as a handle is given a handle or left out, because a plain value
  there reads as a handle that cannot be written.
- **A binding with a `within` step.** The rule for a write edge holds for
  a binding of a pattern compiled in (`site` steps alone) and for a
  binding of an element body (an `element` step) as for a binding with
  no step. Three things differ, and each is where the run of today
  stores something, not what a template holds.
  - **Where the stream is.** The plan does not say where a stream is
    stored (section 1.1, "Where the stream of a binding is stored"). A
    harness finds the stream of a binding by the position at which the
    compiled path's executor recorded that it stored the link, and sends
    the event to the stream that the run of today holds at the same
    position. For a collection among the children of a view node the
    compiled path and the runtime store the same positions (section
    3.4). The JSX factory flattens the children it is given when the
    pattern is built (`children.flat()` in `h` in
    `runtime/runner/src/builder/h.ts`). The result of a `map` over a
    cell is no array at that time, so it is one child, at the position
    the expression is written at, and the stored child holds the
    assembled array. The stream of element `i` is then at `children/k/i`
    followed by the rest of the path, where `k` is the position of that
    child. One case differs. A `map` over a constant array of the
    module, which is a collection over plain values in place, is
    evaluated when the pattern is built, its result is an array, and the
    runtime stores its elements in place among the children, each as a
    child of its own, where the compiled path stores the collection as
    one child. A harness that reads the run of today finds the stream of
    such a binding at the children themselves. At a child position that
    holds the result of a pattern, the runtime's path has `$UI` after
    the position, where the compiled path holds the callee's tree in
    place. A position below a `select` holds no stream while another
    branch is selected, in the run of today as in the compiled path.
  - **Where a state cell or an output of another instance is.** In the
    plan a pattern compiled in has no result cell, and what it declares
    is named by the enclosing instance and the steps of `within`
    (section 1.3). In the runtime each pattern at a tag or a call, and
    each run of an element callback, is an instance with a result
    document of its own. The `internal` metadata of that document lists
    the cells the instance's body made, and their identifiers derive
    from the result cell and the name of the declaration
    (`runtime/runner/src/derived-internal-cell-ids.ts`); its `argument`
    metadata links to the instance's argument document. The plan has no
    record that says where the runtime stores the result of a `site`
    step. The comparison finds the instance among the documents that
    the stored links lead through from the result to the row's
    position: the path of the stream for a write edge, and the path of
    the output for an output.
  - **Where a slot of root `element` is read.** The template's side
    reads an `identity` slot that is the handle of the handler's
    element at the element's position in the source collection, and
    the slot of a handle the element body closes over at the captured
    place (section 2.2). The runtime's transaction reads both in the
    argument document of the element's instance, at `element` and
    below `params`. The rule "The coordinator's join on an element's
    argument document", below, says what a row then differs by.

  A write edge whose target is the stream of another binding, as a
  handler that sends to a stream of its state has, stores nothing at
  the target and is no row. The write of the handler that the stream
  reaches belongs to that handler's own event.
- **An existence entry that an earlier write left.** The runtime's side of
  a row can hold clauses of a write that is not the one the row is about.
  The runtime mints a `derived` entry of class `shape` once, with the join
  of the transaction that created the path, and carries it over every
  later write to a path that still exists; an entry at a path that a write
  removed stays until the path is created again, which the comments of
  `prepareBoundaryCommitSteps` record as a known residual. A value read
  of the written path consumes the `shape` entries at the path and below
  it (section 2.2). The template of a write edge is the label of that one
  write, and it does not hold the existence label of what an earlier
  write stored. So where an earlier event of the scenario created the
  written path, or a path below it, under a label with a clause that the
  later handler did not read, the row is **tighter** by that clause. A row
  is of this kind where every clause that the template lacks is held by a
  `derived` entry of class `shape` that the event's transaction did not
  mint. It is expected, it is counted as tighter, and it is reported apart
  from a row that is tighter because the template leaves out something
  the runtime's join of that write holds. It is no narrowing by the rule
  of the template: the compiled path stores the same `shape` entry
  (section 2.3, "A path that a write edge targets"), so a reader of the
  path consumes the clause in both. The same holds for a row of an
  output.
- **The coordinator's join on an element's argument document.** This is
  a deliberate difference from the runtime of today, by the ruling that
  labels flow per value through the callback of a per-element construct
  (section 3.6). Today the argument document of an element's instance
  carries, on every path, the one join of the coordinator's transaction
  that set the element up, and a handler of the element body is given
  every handle from that document. Its transaction consumes that join:
  with the element's handle the entries at `*`, and the `link` entry at
  `element` where the link has one, and with a captured handle the
  `followRef` entry at `params/*` (section 3.6, "Today, the argument
  document of an element"). The template has none of it. So the write
  row of a handler
  bound in an element body is **tighter** by each clause of that join
  that the handler's own slots do not hold: the clauses of the list's
  own document, and, where the elements are stored in place in that
  document, the clauses of the other elements. A row is of this kind
  where every clause that the template lacks is held by an entry of
  origin `structure` or `link` of the argument document of the
  element's instance that the event's transaction consumed. It is
  expected, it is counted as tighter, and it is reported apart, as a
  row of the rule above is. Unlike that rule it is a narrowing by the
  rule of the template: a reader of the written path consumes the
  clause today and does not in the compiled path.

  A harness that cannot read what a transaction consumed decides the
  condition from what is stored. It takes the clauses of every entry of
  origin `structure` or `link`, at every path, of the argument document
  of each element instance on the way from the result to the handler's
  stream, where that way has one instance for each step of the
  binding's `within`, and it counts a row under this rule where the row
  is tighter and every clause the template lacks is among them. That
  can count a row here whose clause the transaction consumed from
  another entry that holds the same clause.
- **A template with no clause beside the coordinator's join.** Where
  every clause of the run's label is one the rule above takes away, the
  template's label is empty, and a `derive` mints no atom beside an
  empty label (section 3.2, "When `derive` and `fold` mint"). The run's
  join is not empty, so the run stores the atom of the handler's body
  with the write. Such a row is tighter in confidentiality by the
  coordinator's join and looser in integrity by that one atom. A kept
  output in the same position carries the pattern's atom all the same;
  the target of a write edge has no such atom. *Assumed* (section 8,
  question 96): the row is not a row of the rule above. It is counted
  apart, and its category stays looser, in integrity alone. The case is
  a handler bound in an element body that closes over a state cell of
  the pattern alone, where the list declares clauses. The corpus
  comparison met no such row. The handler `askToRetire` of
  `patterns/system/profile-picker/profile-picker.tsx` would be one
  without the assumption of question 85 (section 2.2).
- **The state a row is read on.** The template of a write edge is
  evaluated on what is stored before the event is sent, which is what
  the handler's transaction reads, and the runtime's side is read after
  the event. Evaluated after the event, a slot of a cell that the
  handler both reads and writes has the label of the run's own write,
  which holds every clause the run consumed, and a template that lacks
  one of the handler's reads compares as equal. A row belongs to the
  state that the earlier events of the scenario left: with the events
  sent in another order an event can reach another element or find
  another value stored, and the row's category can differ for that
  reason and for no other. A harness that has no access to the write
  attempts of a transaction, which the runtime releases when the
  transaction settles, takes as written a target whose value differs
  after the event, or that holds more links on the way from its path to
  its value than it held before. The second condition finds a link
  stored in the place of an equal value. A write of an equal value that
  stores no link is not seen, and that edge is counted with the writes
  the run did not make.
- **A label the runtime fails to read.** The runtime's side of a row is
  read with every link followed, and such a read can fail: resolution
  stops at a cycle of links (`resolveLink` in
  `runtime/runner/src/link-resolution.ts` throws there), and
  `cfcLabelViewForResolvedCellWithStatus` in
  `runtime/runner/src/cfc/label-view.ts` then returns what it read
  before the failure and reports that the read failed. A partial label
  is not the runtime's label of the path. *Assumed* (section 8,
  question 88): a row that needs a label the runtime failed to read is
  not a row of the comparison, and it is counted apart by that reason.
  A handler can store such a cycle with `set` and `get` alone: what
  `get` returns for an object is a view of the cell, a `set` of that
  view stores a link, and two cells that each store what the other
  returned link to each other.
- **A written path that holds a link, for an edge with no
  `reference`.** The rule for a write edge joins the template's side
  with what a read through the stored link consumes only for an edge
  with a `reference` member. A run can store a link at the target of an
  edge that has none: the runtime stores a value that carries a stored
  address as a link (section 3.14), and a body can write a value that
  was a reference on this run alone. The runtime's side then has the
  label of the link's target, and at the written path a `followRef`
  stamp and no `value` entry, so it has no atom of the run where the
  template mints the body's. *Assumed* (section 8, question 87): such
  a row is not a row of the comparison and is counted apart, and where
  the plan has an edge with `reference` for the same write, that edge's
  row is the row of the write.

  Whether the run stored a link is decided, without the write attempts,
  by the count of links stored on the way from the path of the target
  to its value: the edge is not compared where the target holds more
  after the event than the fewest it held at any earlier point of the
  scenario. That decision has three limits. A target that held a link
  when it was first read has that count as its fewest, so a link the
  run stores again there is not found. A path that the run added below
  a target, such as a pushed element, is not decided this way, because
  the runtime stores a pushed object through a link of its own. And a
  row that needs a label the runtime fails to read is counted under
  that reason first.

**Which entries are the static part.** *Assumed* (section 8, question 70): the
static part is separated by the origin of a stored entry (`LabelEntryOrigin` in
`runtime/runner/src/cfc/types.ts`) and by the document that holds it, and by
nothing else, because a stored entry does not say which schema declared it.

| Origin | In the comparison |
| --- | --- |
| `declared`, in a document that holds the result of a node: the document an output path names, and each document a reader passes from there on the way to a value that a node computed | The static part. Left out of the runtime's side, and expected as a difference |
| `declared`, in a document that a slot of the template is bound in, or that a reference the output passes on leads to: the argument document of the instance, a cell the argument links to, the document of a state cell, and a cell that a site of a body created | Compared. These are the labels of the places a template reads, which its slots resolve to |
| `derived` | Compared. The stamp of a run's join |
| `structure` | Compared. The stamp of a run, as below |
| `link` | Compared where a slot reads through the link, a write edge targets the handle, or the slot is `resolved`. Left out of the label of an `identity` slot whose handle the body only passes on: the entry holds what the reference declares, which for a link to a cell repeats the label of the cell's type, and by ruling that label is not in the slot (section 2.2). The stamp of the run that wrote the link is an entry of origin `structure`, and it is compared |
| `minted`, `external-ingest` | Compared. Atoms the runtime or a builtin wrote for a value |
| `label-metadata` | Not compared. No read of content consumes it; a `labelMetadata` slot resolves to it (section 2.4) |
| No origin | Compared. An entry written before entries had origins |

A `declared` entry is one of two things, and the document tells them apart.
The static part is what the builder joins onto the outputs of a node from
the schemas of the node's inputs (`applyArgumentIfcToResult` and
`applyInputIfcToOutput`, above), so it is in the document of a node's
result. The other kind is the label that the type of a place declares for
the place itself: the type of an input, the type a state cell is constructed
with, or the type a `createCell` site names. It is in the document of that
cell, which no node writes as its result. A template reads such a place
through a slot, the slot's label holds the entry, and `Slot.declared` is its
lower bound (section 1.5). The same holds for the target of a reference that
an output passes on, which a dereferencing read of the output consumes on
both sides. Leaving such an entry out would remove from the runtime's side a
clause that the template's side has, and the row would read as looser where
the two are equal. The `pinned` output of
`patterns/dev/test/cfc-trusted-write/main.tsx` is the case in the corpus: a
state cell whose own type declares a clause, returned by reference. The one
stored entry that holds the clause is the `declared` entry of the state
cell's document, and the template's side has the clause through the
`identity` slot of the state cell, dereferenced.

So the static part is the `declared` entries of the documents that hold the
result of a node, and no entry of another origin. A label that a node's own
result schema declares is a `declared` entry of the same document, and it is
left out with the static part, because the stored entry does not tell the
two apart. The result document of a child instance is such a document. An
entry of origin `structure` is a stamp of a run,
as a `derived` entry is (`isFlowStageStamp` in
`runtime/runner/src/cfc/prepare.ts`). `prepareBoundaryCommitSteps` in that file
mints every one of them, each with confidentiality that the transaction
consumed and with no clause taken from a schema:

- at the slot of a recorded link write, the transaction's join
  (`observes: "followRef"`);
- at a container, the membership stamp (`observes: "enumerate"`) with the
  transaction's join, or for a result wiring the runtime decides when the graph
  is built, with what the transaction had read when the setup began, joined in
  both cases with what a read declared onward to the container consumed at its
  own path;
- at the `*` child of a container of references, one entry each for
  `shape`, `value` and `followRef` with the same join;
- at a container, once, the existence entry (`observes: "shape"`) with the
  join of the transaction that created it.

A run's join includes the `declared` entries of the documents the run read. A
clause that reaches a result through the static part of one node is therefore
also in the `derived` and `structure` stamps of every node that read that
result, and the separation by origin does not remove it there. That is the case
for the container of a `map` (section 3.6): its membership stamp holds the
coordinator's join, and the template is tighter than that stamp with the
`structure` entries compared.

A scenario that gives an input its label at a cell the argument links to, under
a schema the pattern's argument schema does not hold, has an empty static part
for that label. The comparison of a conditional over such an input shows the
runtime's label without the condition's clauses (section 3.5).

The comparison criterion is the overview's: a template label is **equal or
tighter, never looser**. Tighter means fewer confidentiality clauses, or more
integrity atoms. Each rule that is tighter says what the narrowing rests on.
**There are three exceptions**, all deliberate.

- **The collection index** (section 3.17). A bucket's membership label
  includes the key of every element, where the runtime today stores only
  the labels of the elements in the bucket. Exclusion from a bucket is an
  observation, so the wider label is the correct one.
- **A static read through a handle, on a run that throws before it**
  (section 3.9). A read through a handle is a slot when every run of the
  body that returns normally makes it. A run that throws before reaching
  the read did not make it, and today its transaction does not carry the
  read's label. The template does: the error state of the failed body, or
  the outcome of the failed handler, is labeled with the whole footprint
  (section 5.2), that slot included.
- **The integrity of a default** (section 2.5). A slot that reads as a default
  has the empty integrity, where today the read has the integrity of the entries
  that resolve at the bound address. Fewer integrity atoms is looser. This
  exception is by ruling: no principal wrote the value of a default at the
  place, so no claim stored for the place describes it. A slot that reads a
  stored object whole keeps the object's integrity and is not part of the
  exception. A state cell whose first value is a constant and that
  nothing has written reads as the default of its schema, and is a case
  of this exception (section 1.3).

The stage 3 comparison expects these four differences in that direction
(section 7.5). A promoted `computed` is not a fifth. By ruling it mints no
`TransformedBy` atom for the code of its callback, and every kept output of the
pattern that contains it carries the atom of that pattern (section 3.2, "The
atom of the pattern"). Against today each path of its result has one atom that
names code where the runtime has one, and the two name different code. An
output that the pattern body passes on, with no `computed`, carries the
pattern's atom where the runtime stores none, which is **tighter**. What that
atom's truth rests on is in section 3.2.

### 3.2 Template semantics

For a template `t`, with `sel(i)` the branch the value code reported for
selector `i`:

| Node | `C(t)` | `I(t)` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `const` | empty | neutral for `⊓` |
| `slot s` | `C(s)` | `I(s)`, unchanged |
| `output n` | `C` of the `template` of entry `n` of `Plan.outputs` | `I` of that template, unchanged; neutral where that template is |
| `shared n` | `C` of entry `n` of `Plan.templates`, for the inputs of the place that holds the node | `I` of that entry for those inputs, unchanged |
| `derive` | `⊔` of `C` over `inputs` | `⊓` of `I` over `inputs`, plus `TransformedBy` for `by` |
| `select` | `C(condition) ⊔ C(branches[sel])` | `I(branches[sel])` |
| `fold` | `C(membership) ⊔` the `⊔` of `C(body)` over the elements it covers | `⊓` of `I(body)` over those elements, plus `TransformedBy` for its `pattern` |
| `pick` | `C(choice) ⊔ C(body)` at the chosen child | `I(body)` at the chosen child |
| `dynamic` | `⊔` of the labels the journaled reads consumed | `⊓` over those reads |

The label of a kept output is the label of its template by this table, with
one atom added to the integrity: the `TransformedBy` atom of the pattern the
plan is compiled from ("The atom of the pattern", below).

**A reference to an output.** By ruling a template names the template of
another output and never holds a copy of it. Where an input of a node is
the value of an entry of `Plan.outputs`, kept or interim, the input is
the `output` node that names the entry. The rule holds at every position
that takes a template: an input of a `derive`, the `condition` and a
branch of a `select`, the `body` of a `fold`, the `choice` and the `body`
of a `pick`, a template of a record (`WriteEdge.template`,
`ComputedInput.template`, `Collection.membership`, `Operation.input`,
and the `template` of a path of `Binding.state` and of
`Closure.params`), and the root of `Output.template` where an output
passes the value of another output on. It holds whichever cone computes
the named output, the cone of the template that names it included. The
member names `op: "output"` and `output` are this document's choice.

The ruling is on the templates of outputs. That the templates of the
other records follow it is *assumed,* provisional (P5; section 8,
question 165): every record of section 1.1 that holds a `Template`, the
ones named above and any other, has the `output` node wherever the
template it holds, or an input of that template, is an output of the
plan, and no record holds a copy of the template of an output. It
changes a representation and no label, for the reason "What the node
denotes" gives below. The template of a body, the `derive` over its
footprint (section 3.9), is no output, so each write edge of a body
holds that `derive`, with `output` nodes for the entries of
`Body.computed` that are outputs. Where the `derive` stands at more
than one position, which it does for a body with two write edges, it
is an entry of `Plan.templates` and each position holds a `shared`
node (provisional, P6; "A template written once", below).

- **Which entry is named.** An input that is a path of a value the
  instance computed is the node of the nearest entry at or above the
  path, as the label of a path is the template of that entry (section
  3.4). An input that is a constructed value observed whole is the join
  of the `output` nodes of its entries at and below the path (section
  3.4). A value that only the cone computing it uses has no entry
  (section 1.4), so no node can name it, and its template is written in
  place in the template of what uses it.
- **What the node denotes.** The label of the named output's `template`
  by the table above, and the neutral label where that template
  instantiates to it. It is the label of the template and not of the
  stored output: for a kept output it is without the atom that the rule
  for every kept output adds. So a template with each `output` node
  replaced by the template it names denotes the same label, and the
  ruling changes the meaning of no template.
- **For which inputs.** The node is instantiated for the inputs of the
  template that holds it (section 4.2). A template of an element body
  that names an output of the same body gets the label of that output
  for the same element keys, and one that names an output of an
  enclosing body, or of the pattern body, gets the label for the
  enclosing keys. No template outside an element body names a
  per-element output except under a `fold` or a `pick` over the
  collection, which instantiates its `body` for an element. That is the
  same for a body over an array of references, over an array of plain
  values in place, and over the result of another per-element construct:
  the cases differ in how a key is computed (section 1.3) and not in
  which output a node names.
- **The selections of the named template.** The selections and the
  chosen children that the named template is instantiated under are
  those that the cone computing the named output reported at its last
  evaluation, for the same keys. They are not reported again by the cone
  of the template that holds the node.
- **No cycle.** The references among the outputs of a plan form no
  cycle. A value is computed before it is used, and a cycle of an
  instance goes through a side-write (section 1.4), which its reader
  reads at a slot and not at an output.

**The size of a plan.** No template grows with the template of another
output: an `output` node has one size whatever it names. The size of a
plan is therefore linear in the number of its outputs and of the nodes
of their templates, and does not follow the number of paths by which
one output depends on another. That bounds the templates of a plan
against each other. It does not bound one template against the source
it is written from, because a rule of this section can write one
template at several positions. The next paragraph is on that.

**A template written once.** *Assumed,* provisional (P6; section 8,
question 168): no plan holds the same template twice. The ruling on
`output` nodes removes a copy of the template of an output. Five rules
of this section write a template that is no output at more than one
position:

- `a && b`, `a || b` and `a ?? b` have the template of `a` in the
  condition and in a branch (section 3.5). Where `a` is computed and
  used inside one cone it has no entry of `Plan.outputs`, so a chain of
  `n` operands, each written in place, has about 2 to the power `n`
  nodes.
- A node over constructed values is written once per path, each with the
  condition of the `select` or the choice of the `pick` (section 3.4).
- The template of a body, the `derive` over its footprint, is the
  template of each write edge of the body and of each path of its result
  that has an entry (section 3.9).
- `Collection.membership` of a `map` is the membership its source has
  ("The membership a collection iterates", below), and the parts of an
  index repeat the source's membership joined with a `fold` (section
  3.17). Over an array of references and over an array of plain values
  in place that membership is one `slot` node, which is a leaf. Over the
  result of another per-element construct it is the membership of the
  upstream record, which for a `filter` or a `flatMap` upstream is a
  `fold`.
- A constructed value observed whole is the join of the `output` nodes
  of all its entries, at each place that consumes it (section 3.4).

The plan therefore has a table, `Plan.templates`, and the node `{ op:
"shared"; template: n }`, which stands for entry `n` of the table. The
member names are those of the provisional decision.

- **Which templates are entries.** The compiler first writes every
  template by the rules of this document with nothing shared, each join
  in the form "A join" gives it below. A *position* is a member of a
  record of section 1.1 that holds a `Template`, or a member of a node
  that does. Two templates are equal where they are equal as they are
  written: the same nodes in the same order, with the same indexes of
  slots, outputs, selectors, choice points, collections, bodies,
  patterns and dynamic reads. A template is an entry where it is no leaf
  node (`const`, `slot`, `output` and `dynamic` are the leaf nodes) and
  an equal template stands at another position. The largest are taken
  first: once a template is an entry, what it holds is counted at the
  positions of the entry and not again at each position that names the
  entry, so a part of it is an entry of its own only where it also
  stands somewhere else. Each position of an entry holds the `shared`
  node, and so does the root of `Output.template` where two outputs have
  equal templates. An entry holds `shared` nodes for the entries inside
  it and `output` nodes as any template does. No two entries are equal.
- **It is part of the canonical form.** The compiler has no choice in
  it: a plan in which a template that this rule makes an entry is
