  written in place, or in which an entry is named once, is not a plan of
  this format. One source then has one plan and one plan hash (section
  1.2).
- **The order of the entries** is that of first occurrence in a walk of
  the plan with nothing shared: the members of `Plan` in the order
  section 1.1 declares them, the entries of each in order, the members
  of a record in the order of their declaration, and each template depth
  first with the members of a node in the order of their declaration.
  The order is part of the provisional decision's question, since the
  decision names none.
- **What the node denotes.** The label of the entry by the table above,
  instantiated with the inputs of the place that holds the node: the
  element keys, the selections and the chosen children that the same
  template written in place there is instantiated with. A selector or a
  choice point of an entry is one entry of `Plan.selectors` or of
  `Plan.picks` at every position that names the entry, because equal
  templates have equal indexes. This differs from an `output` node,
  whose selections are those that the cone of the named output reported.
  A template with each `shared` node replaced by its entry denotes the
  same label, so the table changes the meaning of no template.
- **No cycle.** An entry holds entries that are smaller than itself
  alone, so the references among the entries form no cycle, and the
  `output` nodes inside an entry form none for the reason "A reference
  to an output" gives.
- **Once per set of inputs.** The label of an entry is formed at most
  once in a transaction for one set of inputs, and every `shared` node
  that names the entry for that set uses the one result (section 4.1).
- **What it does not reach.** Sharing is inside one plan and between
  equal templates. Two templates that differ in one index are two
  templates. The copies of a pattern that is compiled in at two sites
  have slots, bodies and outputs of their own in the written-out form,
  so they share nothing by this rule, and the records of a plan other
  than its templates are not shared by it either (section 8, question
  168). Provisional (P18): a plan holds such a pattern once, and the
  table is formed per record, for the plan's own lists and for each
  callee (section 1.1, "A pattern compiled in is written once").

With the table the templates of a plan together hold each distinct
template once, and one node for each position that names it. A chain of
`n` operands of `&&` is about `n` `select` nodes and at most `n`
entries, a node over a constructed value of `p` paths holds its
condition once and `p` `shared` nodes, and a body with `W` write edges
holds its `derive` once and `W` `shared` nodes.

**How the table fits the two keys and the join.** The provisional
decision says that the hash, the keys and "the same input of a join"
treat a `shared` node by the identity of its entry, and asks that this
be checked against the provisional decisions P2 and P3. The three are
consistent in the following reading, which is this document's and is
part of question 168.

- *The join (P3).* Equality as written is decided on the templates with
  nothing shared, before the table is formed. Because every repeated
  template that is no leaf is an entry and no two entries are equal, two
  `shared` nodes stand for equal templates exactly where they have one
  index, and a `shared` node never stands for a template that is also
  written in place. So comparing `shared` nodes by index gives the
  answer that comparing the templates as written gives, and P3 holds
  unchanged.
- *The slot-free hash and the two keys (P2).* They treat a `shared` node
  as P2 has them treat an `output` node: as it is written. The hash
  replaces the index by a position (section 1.2), and the instantiation
  key and the memo key hold the identifier of the label of each entry
  that the template reaches under its own selections, and no slot,
  selection or chosen child of the entry (sections 4.1 and 4.3). The
  other reading, in which the hash and the keys are over the template
  with each `shared` node replaced by its entry, would give each key the
  size of the replaced form, which for a chain of `&&` is the size the
  table removes. The table index itself is in no hash of a template,
  since it is a position in one plan.
- *What differs from P2 for an output.* Whether a template is an entry
  depends on what else its plan holds, and whether a value is an output
  depends on the source alone. So the slot-free hash of a template can
  differ between two plans that hold it, which costs a miss of the memo
  across plans and changes no label.

**A rule over a template.** Several rules of this document are stated
over what a template "reaches", "has" or "holds". Each of them is a rule
about the template with every `output` node replaced by the template it
names and every `shared` node by its entry (provisional, P6), so it
follows both nodes, except where the list below says otherwise. By
ruling none of them is computed as a walk of that replaced form as a
tree. Each is computed per output: the result for an output is formed
from the nodes that its own template holds and from the results for the
outputs that its `output` nodes name, and the result for an output is
formed once and used at every node that names it. The same holds per
entry of `Plan.templates`: the result for an entry is formed once, for
one set of inputs where the rule is one of run time, and used at every
`shared` node that names it. Each then costs time linear in the size of
the plan, or of what a transaction instantiates. The last column of the
table says how each rule treats a `shared` node, all of it provisional
(P6).

| Rule | Follows `output` nodes | Formed once per | A `shared` node |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The label of a template (section 4.2) | Yes | Output and set of inputs, in a transaction (section 4.1, "A label is instantiated once") | Followed: the node has the label of its entry for the inputs of the place that holds it. Formed once per entry and set of inputs, in a transaction |
| What makes a demanded output due when a slot's label alone changed (section 4.1, step 1) | Yes: a slot that the template reaches through an `output` node counts | Output | Followed: a slot that an entry holds counts for every output whose template names the entry. Which slots an entry reaches is found once per entry |
| The instantiation key (section 4.1) | No: it holds the label of each output that the template names, and no slot, selection or chosen child of the named template | Template | Not followed: the key holds the identifier of the label of each entry that the template reaches under its own selections, and no slot, selection or chosen child of the entry. An entry has a key of its own |
| The slot-free hash of a template (section 1.2) | No: it is over the template as written | Template | Not followed: the hash is over the template as written, with the index of the node replaced by a position. An entry has a hash of its own |
| `Output.scope` (section 1.4) | Yes | Output, at compile time | Followed: what an entry gives is found once per entry |
| The input constraints that an output lists (section 1.5) | Yes | Output, at compile time | Followed: the constraints of the bodies whose `derive` an entry holds are found once per entry and listed by every output that names it |
| Whether an output of a cone reaches a slot that a constraint of expression code lists (section 1.5) | Yes | Output, at compile time | Followed, once per entry |
| The writer of an output, a `derive` by a body at the root (section 1.5) | Yes, at the root alone | Output, at compile time | Followed at the root alone: an output whose template is a `shared` node has the writer that the root of the entry gives |
| The evaluation of a template on declared labels, and whether it is evaluated at all (sections 1.5 and 4.4) | Yes | Output, at compile time | Followed: an entry is evaluated once, and a template that names an entry which is not evaluated is not evaluated |
| The label of the label-metadata observation of a computed value (section 3.16) | Yes | Output, in a transaction | Followed, with the label of the entry that the transaction formed |
| The labels on a cycle of side-writes (section 4.5) | Yes | Output, in each round | Followed: once per entry and set of inputs, in each round |
| Which staged writes a write uses (section 4.5) | Yes | Output, in a transaction | Followed: the staged writes that an entry's slots resolve to are found once per entry and set of inputs |
| A `const` or a repeated input of a join (below) | No: the inputs are compared as they are written | Node | Compared as written: two `shared` nodes are one input where they name one entry, which is exactly where the templates they stand for are equal as written. A `shared` node is no `const` |
| When a `derive` and a `fold` mint (below) | No: the condition is on the label of the node, which the labels of its inputs give | Node | The node mints nothing. A `derive` and a `fold` of the entry mint as they do written in place, once for each time the label of the entry is formed |

A `select` instantiates the `output` nodes of its condition and of the
selected branch, and none of an unselected branch. A `fold` instantiates
its `body` for each element it covers: an `output` node of the body that
names a per-element output gets that element's label, and one that names
an output outside the element body gets one label, formed once for all
the elements. A `pick` instantiates its `body` for the chosen child, and
an `output` node there gets the label of the named entry with the child
slots bound to that child (section 3.18). A `dynamic` node belongs to the
template that holds it: the label of its journaled reads reaches a
template that names that one only as a part of the named output's label.

A `shared` node is instantiated where the same template written in place
is: a `select` forms the label of an entry that its condition or its
selected branch names and of none that an unselected branch alone names,
a `fold` forms the label of an entry in its `body` for each element it
covers, and a `pick` for the chosen child. A `dynamic` node of an entry
belongs to the entry, and its journaled reads are those of the place
that holds the `shared` node.

**The atom of the pattern.** By ruling, trust is attached to a pattern, and
the code of the reactive tier is named in a `TransformedBy` atom by the
pattern that contains it. The atom's `identity` is an entry of
`Plan.patterns` (section 1.5). Two rules place it.

- **What expression code computes.** A `derive` with
  `by: { expression: true }` and a `fold` mint the atom of the pattern in
  whose source the expression or the construct is written: entry `pattern`
  of `Plan.patterns`, and entry 0 where the node has no `pattern` member.
  Every expression of one pattern mints one atom, whichever cone evaluates
  it. For code of a pattern compiled into another under a `site` step, that
  is the pattern compiled in and not the one that holds the site, so an
  expression mints the same atom in every plan that holds it: by ruling
  (2026-11-19; section 8, question 64), code of a pattern B compiled into a
  pattern A mints B's atom. In this
  document, "`by: { expression: true }`" names such a node whatever its
  `pattern` member is. Where a rule forms a join, `pattern` is the pattern
  in whose source the construct the rule applies to is written.
- **Every kept output.** Every entry of `Plan.outputs` with `kept: true`
  carries the atom of entry 0 of `Plan.patterns`, the pattern of the
  instance, whatever its template is. That holds for a value the pattern
  only passes on, through a `slot`, a `select`, or a `pick`, as for one it
  computes. No template node stands for it: it is a rule on `Output`, and
  the runtime adds the atom where it instantiates the label of a kept
  output (section 4.1). The atom is added with no condition, so a kept
  output whose template has no label carries it too. Where the template is
  a `derive` or a `fold` of the same pattern, the atom added is the atom
  the node minted, and the output carries it once.
- **Every commit is prepared.** By ruling (2026-11-19; section 8,
  question 177), every commit of a compiled pattern is prepared when the
  experimental option is on, a commit that reads no labeled data included,
  so every kept output it writes carries the atom. The owner's reason: soon
  all data carries a label, at least a `User` or `Space` atom. Measured over
  the corpus in milestone 4 of the integration, preparing every commit
  raised the preparations from 407 to 2,280 and the preparation time from
  379 ms to 690 ms, about 0.3 ms per added preparation. Milestone 4 of
  the integration builds it: a transaction that records an authorized
  write record of a plan is prepared.

**Where the atom of a kept output is stored.** A kept output that holds a value
has the atom in the label of the value. A kept output that passes a value on by
reference stores a link. By ruling (2026-11-20; Z81 of the continuation plan)
the pattern's atom is joined onto the content there, with no scope, so a read
through the link takes it. The owner's words: "i think (c) is fine, i see it as
lacking coarseness in differentiating selected vs computed, but what integrity
means is really in a semantic space the pattern author owns / what this
integrity means is anyway up for interpretation and passing through a selection
just has low meaning". The atom is therefore no endorsement scoped to the
selection: a reader cannot tell from it whether the pattern computed the value
or chose it, and "What the atom of a kept output rests on" below says what it
claims in both cases.

The stored form: the atom is in the label that a read of the value at the output
path consumes, which is an entry of the class `value` at that path in the
document that holds the link, with a `shape` entry beside it. A read of the
output that follows the link joins that entry with the integrity of the target.
Nothing is written to the envelope of the document the link names: the target
keeps its own entries, a reader that reaches the target through another
reference does not take the atom, and another output or another instance that
refers to the same target says nothing about this pattern. Where the links of
the elements of an array have one label, one entry at the array's `*` path holds
it (section 2.3). The label of such a path is stored in the same place whether
the document that holds it is written whole or the path is written alone.
Milestone 4 of the integration builds it (`prepareBoundaryCommitSteps` of
`runtime/runner/src/cfc/prepare.ts`).

The specification's rule for the integrity of a link is §3.7.2
(`03-core-concepts.md`), which scopes the endorsement of a link to the
selection. The ruling stores no scoped endorsement. What it leaves open is in
section 8, question 72: whether the specification needs a sentence for an atom
with no scope at the path of a link, and whether a write edge that stores a
reference follows the same rule. The owner has confirmed (2026-11-19) that every
kept output carries the atom. *Assumed* (section 8, question 71): the atom of an
instance is the same at every kept output, so it is stored as one entry at the
root of each document the keep set is stored in, which applies at every path
below, and not as one entry per output.

**What the atom of a kept output rests on.** For a value the pattern passes on,
the atom is integrity that the runtime does not store today, and "tighter means
more integrity atoms" (section 3.1) covers it only if the atom is true. It
claims that the code of the named pattern decided what this output holds: which
value, selected from which inputs. It does not claim that the pattern computed
the value. A read of the output takes the atom beside the integrity of the value
passed on, and the stored label of the value itself, at its own address, stays
what it was. Three things make the claim true. The plan is compiled from the
pattern's source by a trusted compiler (section 7.2), and its hash is part of
the identity of the compiled pattern. The paths of the result are written by the
runtime alone, from the plan: no body and no other instance writes a kept
output. And the pattern's identity changes when its module does (section 1.5). A
rule that releases on `TransformedBy` of a pattern therefore releases whatever
the pattern passes on as well as what it computes, and an author who names a
pattern in a rule endorses its selections.

**What does not get the atom.** The ruling names the outputs of a pattern.
*Assumed* (section 8, question 71): an interim output, the target of a write
edge, the argument of a child, the request of an effect, and the state of a
binding get no atom added. Each carries the label of its template, which
holds the pattern's atom where a `derive` or a `fold` of the pattern
computed the value, and no atom of the pattern where the value is passed on.
A child's argument is the case that decides the assumption: a pattern
compiled into its caller has no stored argument, so an atom added to a
`Child`'s argument would make a label depend on which of the two forms the
compiler chose. A design the owner proposed for the value a pattern passes on
from an argument, not built and needing a specification change of its own, is
section 8, question 176: the minimum integrity that a pattern declares on an
input is a requirement on the link written for the argument, so the pattern's
atom on a value passed through never vouches for an input below that
minimum.

**The inputs of a `derive`.** A join and a meet do not depend on the order
of their operands or on how often one occurs, so `inputs` is a list for the
sake of the canonical form alone (section 1.2), and the compiler fills it
in one order.

- For expression code, one input per operand, in source order. An operand
  written twice is two inputs, and a constant operand is one `const` node
  each time it is written. Two inputs that are equal and no leaf are two
  `shared` nodes that name one entry (provisional, P6).
- For a body, the `slot` nodes of `Body.reads` in that order, then the
  templates of `Body.computed` in that order, then one `dynamic` node per
  entry of `Plan.dynamicReads` the use of the body made, in the order of
  `Plan.dynamicReads`. Each occurs once.

**A join.** `Template` has no node of its own for a join. Where a rule of
this document says that a template is one template "joined with"
another, or is "the join of" several, the template is a `derive` with
`by: { expression: true }` whose `inputs` are the joined templates, in
the order the rule names them. Its confidentiality is the join. Its
integrity is the meet of the inputs' hereditary atoms, plus the
`TransformedBy` atom of the pattern the construct is written in ("The atom
of the pattern", above). That holds for the membership of a derived
collection too: which elements are present was computed, and the atom
says by what. Three cases need no such node.

- A join with `const` is the other template alone. An `output` node is
  no `const` node, also where the template it names is `const`.
- A join of one template with itself is that template. *Assumed,*
  provisional (P3; section 8, question 164): two inputs are the same
  template where they are equal as they are written, so two `output`
  nodes are the same where they name one output, and two nodes that
  name two outputs with equal templates are two inputs. The label is
  the same either way, because a join and a meet are idempotent. Two
  `shared` nodes are the same where they name one entry (provisional,
  P6), which is the same test, since no two entries are equal ("A
  template written once", above).
- A `fold` joins the membership its collection iterates by its own rule
  (below), so "a `fold` of `t`, joined with membership" is the `fold`
  alone.

Where the node that holds the join uses its confidentiality alone, as the
`condition` of a `select` and the `choice` of a `pick` do, the integrity
of the `derive` has no effect.

**A join or expression code.** The two differ in what they do with a
`const` input and with an input that occurs twice, so each `derive` with
`by: { expression: true }` is one or the other, and the place it comes
from decides which.

- It is expression code where the node stands for something the author
  wrote that computes a value from operands: an operator, a call of a
  member of the standard-library surface, a template literal, and a
  conversion. Its inputs are the operands as written, a `const` operand
  and a repeated operand included, by the rule for expression code
  above. So the node of `count + 1` has two inputs, and one of them is
  `const`.
- It is a join everywhere else: wherever a rule of this document, of
  `builtin-inventory.md`, or of `footprint-analysis.md` forms one
  template from several with the words "joined with" or "the join of".
  That covers a condition or a choice that joins several observations,
  a membership that joins a `shape` or a key, a constructed value
  observed whole (section 3.4), and the positions after a spread. The
  three cases above apply to it: a `const` input and a repeated input
  are left out, and one input left is the template itself, with no
  `derive` around it.

An operand of expression code that is itself a join is one input, the
joined template. The two forms give one label where no input is `const`
or repeated. They differ in the canonical form of the plan, and so in
its hash, which is why the rule is fixed.

**The membership a collection iterates.** A `fold` names a `Collection`,
and `body` is over that record's `element` slots. The membership the
`fold` joins, `C(membership)` in the table, is the label of which
elements the callback is evaluated over and in what order. It is given by
the record's `source`:

| `Collection.source` | The membership the record iterates |
| --- | --- |
| `slot` | The `slot` node of the `enumeration` slot at the source's path |
| `collection` | The `membership` of that record |
| `operation` | The membership of the bucket (section 3.17) |
| `output` | The template of the output's own `enumeration`: for an assembled entry its `template`, for an array constructed in place the template of its container entry (section 3.4), and for the result of one opaque call the call's template |

`Collection.membership` is a different thing: the label of which elements
the *result* of the construct has. For a `map` the two are the same. Where
they are the same and no leaf node, which is a `map` over the result of a
`filter` or a `flatMap`, the template is an entry of `Plan.templates` and
both records hold its `shared` node (provisional, P6). Over an array of
references and over an array of plain values in place the membership is one
`slot` node. For a `filter` and a `flatMap`, `membership` is a `fold` that
names the record itself (section 3.7), and that `fold` joins what the record
iterates, so the definition is not circular. `TemplateInputs.membership` of
section 4.2 returns the membership the record iterates.

Notes on the integrity column:

- **`slot` keeps every class of atom.** It is a pass-through, and §3.1.6.2
  (`03-core-concepts.md`) says of pass-through and exact copy that "the output
  integrity at the path MUST be the input integrity unchanged, across **all**
  propagation classes".
- **`derive` drops value-bound atoms and mints.** This is the default
  transition of §8.9.3 applied to the template's inputs instead of to a
  transaction's reads. The minted atom names `Body.code` for a sandboxed
  body, and the pattern for emitted expression code (section 1.2).
- **A promoted `computed`.** By ruling, a `computed` that meets the promotion
  criterion (`language-subset.md` §6.1) mints no `TransformedBy` atom for the
  code of its callback. It is compiled as expression code of the reactive
  tier, and its templates are those the same expression has when it is written
  in the pattern body. A `derive` in it mints the atom of the pattern that
  contains the `computed`, under the condition below. A path of it whose
  template is a `slot`, a `select`, or a `pick` carries the integrity of what
  it passes on, and, where the path is a kept output, the atom of the pattern
  by the rule for every kept output. Today a `computed` is a lift: one
  transaction writes its whole result, and every path of the result carries an
  atom that names the callback where the join is not empty (section 3.1): the
  module's identity, and the name the transformer gave the callback when it
  moved the call to module scope (section 1.5). So a kept path of the promoted
  result has an atom that names the pattern where the runtime has one that
  names the callback, and it has that atom beside an empty label, where the
  runtime has none. The comparison takes the two atoms as corresponding
  (section 3.1). A path of the promoted result that is an interim output and
  passes a value on has no atom where the runtime has one. Nothing stores the
  label of an interim output. Where such a value reaches a kept output, the
  output carries the pattern's atom, and where a `derive` reads it, the
  `derive` mints. Where it reaches the argument of a child, the target of a
  write edge, or the request of an effect unchanged, what is stored there has
  no atom of the pattern, where today it refers to a result that has the
  callback's atom. That is fewer atoms, under the assumption of "What does not
  get the atom" above, and it is the difference question 71 of section 8 is
  about. A `computed` that stays a body keeps its atom: its
  template is a `derive` whose `by` names `Body.code`, and a kept output of it
  carries the pattern's atom beside that one.
- **`const` is neutral.** A literal is not an observation, so it does not
  empty the meet. This matches the runtime, where a literal in a function
  body is not a read.
- **When `derive` and `fold` mint.** By ruling (2026-11-19; section 8,
  question 66): the atom is minted where the label of the node has a
  confidentiality clause or a hereditary atom, and not beside an empty label.
  That is the condition the runtime applies (section 3.1), so the integrity is
  **equal**. The condition is on the label of
  the node alone. A label that the schema of a written path declares is a
  `declared` entry stored beside the template's label, and it does not make a
  node mint: `deriveFlowJoinImpl` decides on the transaction's join, before the
  declared entries of the targets are added. The condition does not apply to
  the atom of a kept output, which is added in every case. A template that is
  tighter than today down to the empty label, as a test of an absent optional
  field is (section 6.4), mints nothing where the runtime mints beside the
  clauses it holds. Where that value is a kept output it carries the pattern's
  atom all the same, and where it is interim no label is stored for it. Where
  it is the target of a write edge, the stored value has no atom where the
  runtime stores one, which is looser in integrity; section 3.1 ("A template
  with no clause beside the coordinator's join") has the one case found, and
  how such a row is counted is *assumed* (section 8, question 96).
- **Witness-bearing atoms.** *Assumed* (section 8, question 67): a `derive` and
  a `fold` mint, beside the atom that holds the identity alone, one atom with
  the identity and an `inputWitness` for each `TransformedBy` atom that every
  input with a confidentiality clause carries, by the functions the runtime uses
  (section 3.1): the atoms `retainedInputWitnesses` keeps of each such input's
  integrity, met across those inputs by `meetInputWitnesses`, to the nesting
  depth `INPUT_WITNESS_MAX_DEPTH` allows. A node with no input that has a clause
  mints no such atom. The inputs are the node's own, a slot or a nested template
  each, where the runtime takes the locations a transaction read. Without these
  atoms a `derive` over the result of a `derive` would carry one atom where the
  runtime stores two, which is looser.
- **`select` does not combine its branches.** The result *is* the selected
  branch's value, so integrity is that branch's. The condition contributes
  confidentiality only, which is the flow-path rule of §8.11.3
  (`08-11-content-vs-flow-labels.md`): "When data flows through a decision
  point influenced by labeled inputs, the *decision itself* inherits that
  label." Condition integrity is control integrity (§3.4), which the
  specification keeps apart from value integrity.

### 3.3 Property access

`a.b` on an input is not an operation. It extends the slot's path: the
template is `slot (root, path + b, class)`.

`a.b` on a derived value selects the sub-template at `b` when the producer has
per-path templates (object construction, section 3.4). When the producer is
one opaque call, every path of its result has the call's template.

**Today.** A read at a path consumes the entries resolved at that path
(section 2.2), so a node that reads only `a.b` already gets only that label.
**Equal.** The difference is that no node, transaction or document exists for
the access.

### 3.4 Object and array construction

`{ x: e1, y: e2 }` and `[e1, e2]` produce a template per path: the template of
path `x` is the template of `e1`. The container's own `shape` and
`enumeration` are `const` when the key set is static, and otherwise the
template of whatever decides it (a spread of a labeled object, a conditional
key).

**A spread in an object literal.** `{ ...a, x: e }` has, at each path `p` that
the type of `a` declares and no later member of the literal overwrites, the
template of `a.p`. Where `a` is at a slot root the path is passed by
reference, so the template is the `slot` node of the reference at `a.p`. A
member written after the spread replaces the path. A member written before the
spread is replaced where the type of `a` declares its path as required, and
stays where the type does not declare the path. Where the type declares the
path as optional, the result holds the member of `a` when `a` has one and the
earlier member otherwise: the path is a `select` whose condition is the
`shape` of `a.p`. The key set is `const` where the type of `a` is an object
type with no index signature, joined with the `shape` of each optional
property. Where the type of `a` is a record type, whose keys are data, the
result's `enumeration` is that of `a`, and the template at `*` is the template
of `a` at `*`, joined with the templates of the written members whose names
the record's key type admits.

**A spread in an array literal.** `[e0, ...xs, e1]` is an array the cone
computes, and the positions after a spread are not known when the pattern
is compiled. Its `enumeration` is `derive` by expression code over the
`enumeration` of each spread operand. A member written before the first
spread has its own path and the template of its expression. *Assumed*
(section 8, question 51): every position from the first spread on is at
the path `*`, and the template there is the join of the template of each
spread operand at `*`, of the templates of the members written after the
first spread, and of the array's `enumeration`, which says where each
landed. An element that comes from a spread operand is passed by
reference. *Assumed* (section 8, question 159): over an array of plain
values in place that is a reference by key, as for every node of the
reactive tier that passes an element on. A spread of a value of tuple
type has static positions and is the members written out. A spread
attribute in JSX (`language-subset.md` §4.5) is a spread in the object
literal of the attributes. The children of a view node are not such an
array literal: a collection among them is one child ("A JSX element",
below).

**A hole.** `[a, , b]` has a constant key set. The position of the hole
holds nothing, has no template, and contributes nothing to a `fold` over
the array (section 3.8). A collection over the array gives the position no
element key and no cone instance (section 1.3).

**A computed key.** A key that is static in the sense of
`language-subset.md` §4.3 is the name it evaluates to. The path segment
is that string: for a string or a number literal and for a template
literal with no substitution, its text; for a module-scope constant, its
value; and for a well-known key, the string the API's constant holds, so
`[UI]` is the segment `$UI` and `[NAME]` is `$NAME` (`UI` and `NAME` in
`base/api/index.ts`). A key that is not
static is refused there (`reactive:unsupported-expression`), so the plan
has no record for one.

**A JSX element.** A host element is the construction of its view node,
the record the JSX factory returns (`h` in
`runtime/runner/src/builder/h.ts`): `type` and `name`, which are
constants, `props`, the object literal of the attributes, and `children`,
the array literal of the children. So the template of the path
`props/title` of an element is the template of the expression written
at the attribute `title`, and the template of `children/0` is that of
the first child. By ruling a collection among the children, the
assembled result of a `map` among them, is stored as one nested child,
as the runtime of today stores the result of a `map`: the collection
is the child at the position `n` it is written at, whether it is
written as an expression or as a spread child, and the template of
`children/<n>/*` is that of its elements (section 3.6). The children
array is not stored flat, so every child has a static position, a
child written after a collection included, and two collections among
the children of one node are two child positions. The rule is the
same for a collection over an array of references, over an array of
plain values in place, and over the result of another per-element
construct. An array literal that the author writes among the children
is no collection: its members are written out among the children when
the tree is built, each at a child position of its own, as the JSX
factory does today (`children.flat()` in `h`). The runtime of today
stores the same paths for a `map` over a cell (section 3.1, "A binding
with a `within` step"). For a `map` over an array that is written in
place in the pattern body, which is a collection over plain values in
place, this design stores one nested child as well. By the
prototype's comparison the runtime of today runs such a `map` when
the pattern is built and holds its elements as children of their own,
from the position of the expression on.

Two further forms among the children are ruled: each is one child at
the position it is written at.

- **A spread child,** `{...xs}`, holds what `xs` is, as the expression
  child `{xs}` does: the nested collection where `xs` is a collection,
  over an array of references, over an array of plain values in place
  or over the result of another per-element construct, and the
  reference where `xs` is another expression of array type.
- **An array literal that itself has a spread or a hole,** as
  `{[head, ...xs.map(f), tail]}`, is one nested child: an array value
  with a spread, stored at `children/<n>` as one nested array value,
  whose positions are those of any array value with a spread ("A
  spread in an array literal", above). Its members are not written
  out among the children. The same whether `xs` is a collection over
  an array of references, over an array of plain values in place, or
  the result of another per-element construct.

Every child written after either form then has a static position. The
JSX factory of today writes the members out when the tree is built,
for what is an array at that time. An expression of array type that
is no collection, as an input written `{items}`, is one child that
holds the reference, by the rule for any child. The prototype's
compiler makes each of these one child. The runtime of today runs
neither ruled form where a pattern's body writes it over a pattern
value, so the two rules have no run of today's runtime to be compared
with in the reactive tier. For an array literal with a spread among
the children, today's transformer reports that the spread is not
lowerable (`rewriteTrackedOpaquePatternBody` in
`base/ts-transformers/src/transformers/pattern-body-reactive-root-lowering.ts`).
For a JSX spread child of a pattern value, by the prototype's run the
evaluation of the pattern throws. In a function body both forms run
today, a view node flattens the arrays it is handed in both runtimes,
and the prototype's comparison finds the values equal there. The
prototype tried the spread of a pattern value, and its notes do not
say what the runtime of today does for each of the three cases of a
source: an array of references, an array of plain values in place,
and the result of another per-element construct.
A fragment is the same record with the fragment's
name. The rendered tree under `$UI` is such a construction, and its paths
are these.

**The entries of a constructed value.** A constructed value is a record
or an array written in place, a JSX element included. It has no one
template. In `Plan.outputs`, where the plan has entries for it at all
(section 1.4), it has these:

- **A container entry** at the path of the constructed value itself. Its
  `template` is the template of the value's key set: `const` where the
  key set is static, and otherwise the template of what decides it, as
  the first paragraph of this section says. The entry is left out where
  no one cone computes the value and its key set is static: the object a
  pattern body returns, and a record or an array written directly in a
  pattern body or in that object, whose members are each computed by a
  cone of their own or name a slot (section 1.4). Such a value has an
  entry per member and nothing else, and a path with no entry at or
  above it is constant. Where the key set of such a value is not static,
  the container entry is an output of the cone `result`.
- **One entry for each member that is not constructed in place and whose
  template is not `const`,** at the path of the member below the
  constructed value, with the template of the member's expression. A
  member that is itself constructed in place has entries by these rules
  at its own paths, and a container entry of its own only where its key
  set is not static.

The label of a path of the value is the template of the nearest entry at
or above the path. So a path with no entry of its own below a
construction with a static key set is constant, and every path of the
result of one opaque call has the call's template (section 3.3). The
entries have the `cone`, the `kept` and the `interim` of the value: a
record that a promoted `computed` named `stats` returns has entries at
paths below the interim name `stats`.

**A node whose result is a constructed value** is written once per path.
A `select` one of whose branches is a constructed value, a `pick` whose
chosen child is one, and the per-element output of a `map` whose
callback returns one are not one template over the whole value. For each
path at which some branch has an entry, the plan has an entry whose
template is the node with each branch replaced by that branch's template
at the path: the template of the nearest entry of the branch at or above
the path, and `const` where the branch is a constructed value that has
no such path, because the path then holds nothing. Where the branch, the
condition or the choice is an output of the plan, each per-path node has
the `output` node of that entry there and no copy of its template
(section 3.2, "A reference to an output"). Where the condition or the
choice is computed in the same cone and is no leaf node, it is an entry
of `Plan.templates`, and each per-path node has the `shared` node of
that entry (provisional, P6; section 3.2, "A template written once").
The entries of one `select` name one selector, and those of one `pick`
one choice point. The container entry is the node over the container
entries of the branches. For `c ? { x: a } : { x: b, y: d }` the path
`x` has `select(c, [a, b])`, the path `y` has `select(c, [const, d])`,
and the container entry has `select(c, [const, const])`, the label of
which key set the value has.

**A constructed value observed whole.** Where a rule needs one template
for all of a constructed value, the template is the join (section 3.2)
of the templates of its entries at and below the observed path, the
container entry included. That is the case for an operand of expression
code that consumes the whole value, as a substitution of a template
literal does (section 3.19); for an entry of `Body.computed` of class
`value` at or above the constructed value (section 3.9); for a path of
an effect's request or of a child's argument that the value is written
to whole; and for the `body` of a `fold` over elements that are
constructed values. Where the value has entries in `Plan.outputs`, the
inputs of the join are the `output` nodes of those entries, and no copy
of a template. Where two places consume one constructed value whole, the
join is an entry of `Plan.templates` and each place holds its `shared`
node (provisional, P6; section 3.2, "A template written once"). An entry
of `Body.computed` of class `shape` or `enumeration` at the path of a
constructed value has the template of its container entry alone. A
constructed value has no reference, so an `identity` entry there has the
container entry's template too.

**A node over constructed values, observed whole.** Where the value is the
result of a node written once per path, a `select`, a `pick`, or the
per-element output of a `map`, the template is not the join of the per-path
nodes. It is the one node over the branches, each observed whole by this
rule: `select(c, [A, B])` with `A` the join of the entries of the first
branch and `B` that of the second, under the selector the per-path entries
name; a `pick` whose `body` is the chosen child observed whole; and for the
body of a `fold`, the element observed whole. The confidentiality is the
same as that of the join of the per-path nodes, since each of them holds
the condition or the choice and one branch. The integrity is that of the
selected branch observed whole, without the further `derive` a join of
`select` nodes would add, and the template has one node where the join has
one per path.

*Assumed* (section 8, question 53): the entries are as fine as this, one
per member that computes, for the rendered tree too. That one template
over the whole value is not the rule follows from "equal to or tighter":
it would give every member the join of all of them, where the builder
gives each member of a record written in a pattern body the label of its
own node.

**Today.** In a pattern body, a constructed object is structure: each member
is a link to the node that computes it, and each node output is a document
with its own label. **Equal**, at the cost of a document per member. Inside a
`computed` that returns an object, one transaction writes every path, so
every path carries the join of everything the body read. A promoted
expression gets a template per path instead. **Tighter**; this rests on the
compiler (section 7).

### 3.5 Conditional selection

`c ? a : b` produces `select` with `condition` the template of `c` and two
branches. `a && b` is `select(a, [b, a])`: when `a` is falsy the result is
`a` itself. `a || b` and `??` are analogous.

The operand that is both the condition and a branch is written once.
Where it is an output of the plan, both positions hold its `output`
node. Where it is computed inside the cone and is no leaf node, it is an
entry of `Plan.templates` and both positions hold its `shared` node
(provisional, P6; section 3.2, "A template written once"), so the
template of a chain `a && b && c` and longer grows by one `select` for
each operand and not by a factor of two.

The condition's slots have the class the test needs: `value` at the root for
a scalar condition, `shape` at the root for a record or array, whose
truthiness is its existence. Nothing below the root is observed (section
2.4). The static type of the condition decides: `value` where it is a
scalar type, and `shape` where it is a record, an array, a handle, or
`unknown`. At a position of handle or reference type the `shape` slot is
in place (section 2.5).

Three more tests of expression code observe less than the value, by the
rules `footprint-analysis.md` §3.2 gives a function body.

- A comparison with `undefined` or `null`, `==` and `!=` included, reads
  the other operand for `shape`.
- `typeof e` reads `e` for `shape`: the kind of the value and not its
  content.
- `a?.b` tests whether `a` is present, so it reads `a` for `shape`, and
  that observation joins the template of the expression code the access
  is written in. The access itself extends the path (section 3.3).

`a ?? b` tests presence, so the condition is `a` read for `shape`, and
the branch that is `a` is the operand passed on: its `value` where it is
a scalar, and the `slot` node of its reference where it is a container or
a handle.

**A guard in a promoted `computed`.** An `if` in the block body of a
promoted `computed` (`language-subset.md` §6.1) is a `select` over what
its two paths return. A path that ends in a `return` without an
expression, and the path of a guard that has no `else` and falls through
to a `return` of that kind, has the branch `const`.

When the selected arm of `&&` or `||` *is* the condition, the result carries
that operand's full template, not only its truthiness.

The result is the selected operand itself, not a copy: a reference stays the
same reference, and a default declared on the operand's schema reaches
readers of the result, as it does today.

The callable forms `ifElse`, `when` and `unless` are not operations of their
own. Where the compiler still accepts them it maps each to this operation,
and the `str` tag to a template literal (section 3.19).

The unselected branch contributes nothing. Its slots are in the cone's slot
list (section 1.1, `Cone.slots`), which lists what the value function may
receive over all selections. A slot that only the unselected branch reads
is not read, and so makes no cone instance stale
(`execution-and-storage.md` §2.2). The value and the instantiated label of
the result are functions of the condition and the selected branch alone.

**Today.** `ifElse`, `when` and `unless` share `forwardReference`
(`runtime/runner/src/builtins/forward-reference.ts`). Its action reads the
condition's truthiness at its root (`readsTruthyAtRoot` in
`runtime/runner/src/schema.ts`), resolves only the selected input, and makes
two writes in one transaction.

- It writes a reference to the selected input's resolved target into a result
  store the node owns (`ownedCell` in
  `runtime/runner/src/builtins/runtime-owned-store.ts`), at the store's root,
  with `setRawUntyped`. Where the selected input is a literal, the reference is
  a `data:` link, which `setRawUntyped` stores as the literal's value
  (`findAndInlineDataUriLinks`).
- Through `sendResult` it writes a link to that store at the node's output
  binding (`sendValueToBindingInner` in
  `runtime/runner/src/pattern-binding.ts`, under `preserveLinkOutput`), with
  `writeValueOrThrow`, and only where the binding does not hold that link
  already.

The read of the condition is an ordinary read, so the transaction's join
(`deriveFlowJoinImpl`) holds the condition's label. Where that join is stored
depends on what the result store holds.

- **The selected branch is a reference.** No entry holds the join. Neither
  write records a link write: `recordLinkWritePolicyInput`
  (`runtime/runner/src/data-updating.ts`) is reached from `diffAndUpdate`
  alone, and both writes bypass it. `prepareBoundaryCommitSteps` stamps the
  join's confidentiality on the slot of a recorded link write, as a
  `structure` entry with `observes: "followRef"`, and has no such record for
  either slot. Its flow stage then takes each written value as link structure
  (`isPureLinkStructure`), which gets no `derived` entry, and a link at the
  root of a document is no container (`pureLinkContainerPaths`), so it gets no
  `structure` entry either. The two probes `forwardReference` and
  `setRawUntyped` make to elide a write are marked `internalVerifierRead` (in
  `forwardsNothingToUnwrittenStore` and in `setRawUntyped`), so they add
  nothing to the join and are not the cause.
- **The selected branch is a literal.** The result store holds the literal's
  value, which is content. The flow stage stamps the join at the store's root,
  as a `derived` entry that a `value` read consumes and one that a `shape`
  read consumes. No `TransformedBy` atom was observed on either.

A reader of the output path follows the link at the output binding to the
result store, and the reference there to the selected branch, and consumes the
label of the selected branch at the branch's own document. So which label of
the condition reaches a reader is as follows.

| The condition's label is | Selected branch a reference | Selected branch a literal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Declared by the schema of the condition's input | Reaches the reader through the static part alone | Reaches the reader through the static part and the `derived` entries |
| Stored and not declared, as a `derived` entry on the result of another node is | Does not reach the reader | Reaches the reader through the `derived` entries |

The static part of section 3.1 is an entry of origin `declared` at the root of
the document the output binding names, with the declared confidentiality of the
condition and of both branches, whichever branch is selected. Read by origin
without that entry, a conditional over references carries the selected
branch's label and nothing of the condition.

These statements were read from the functions named and observed by running a
pattern over a condition with a stored label, with literal branches and with
branches that are cells, and over a condition whose input schema declares a
clause.
`runtime/runner/test/condition-builtin-reads.test.ts` asserts the literal case
alone ("stamps the sealed clause on an `ifElse` output").

**Against the template.** Which branch a conditional selects reveals the
condition, so the `select` joins the condition's confidentiality, by the
flow-path rule section 3.2 cites. The runtime's own rule for a written
reference is the same: the comment on the link stamp in
`prepareBoundaryCommitSteps` says that a written reference is a selection made
under what the attempt observed, and that the join's confidentiality reaches
its slot. A conditional over references does not get that stamp, because its
writes are not recorded as link writes. That is a **finding against the
runtime**, and the template does not reproduce it.

*Assumed* (section 8, question 69): the template stands, and the comparison for
a conditional is made with the runtime's static part included. With it, the
template is **equal** where the selected branch and the condition carry every
clause the unselected branch declares, and **tighter** where the unselected
branch declares a clause they lack, which is the difference the ruling of
section 3.1 expects. Without it the template has the condition's clauses and
the runtime's label has none of them, which reads as looser and is the
runtime's omission. Where the condition's label is stored and not declared,
the static part does not hold it, and the comparison reports the template as
looser for a conditional over references: that row is the finding, and is not
a fifth exception.

**A conditional written in a `computed`.** `c ? a : b` in the body of a
`computed` is part of a lift today. Its transaction reads the condition and both
operands, writes a copy of the selected value, and mints `TransformedBy` under
the condition of section 3.1. Where the `computed` is promoted
(`language-subset.md` §6.1), the template is a `select` over the operands. Its
confidentiality is equal where the selected branch carries every clause the
other does, and tighter otherwise. The integrity of the `select` is the selected
branch's alone, and by ruling no atom names the callback. Where the conditional
is a kept output it carries the atom of the pattern that contains the
`computed`, by the rule for every kept output of section 3.2: in the label of
the value where the output holds one, and in the label of the content at the
output path where the selected branch is passed on by reference. The runtime's
copy carries the atom of the callback. The comparison takes the two atoms as
corresponding (section 3.1), so the integrity is **equal** where the join is not
empty and **tighter** where it is empty. The same conditional written in the
pattern body, with no `computed`, has the same template and the same atom, where
the runtime mints none: **tighter**.

### 3.6 `map`

`xs.map((x) => body)` creates a `Collection` and compiles `body` once against
`element` slots.

- **Element template.** The template of output path `p` of element `i` is the
  body's template for `p`, with `element` slots bound to element `i`. It
  includes two slots at the element's root: `shape`, which is the element's
  membership in the collection, and `identity`, which is the reference at
  slot `i` when elements are links. Captured outer values are ordinary slots.
- **Membership template.** For a `map` over an input collection, the
  `enumeration` slot of that collection. `map` preserves the domain, so the
  result's membership is its source's.
- **Index.** A node of the body that reads the index reads the slot of
  root `index` that names the collection (section 1.3), and has the
  `slot` node of that slot in its template. The node resolves to the
  label of the collection's array (section 2.2), which for a collection
  over a slot is the collection's `enumeration` joined with the label
  of which link each position holds, because an element's index depends
  on the order of the others. It holds nothing of what a link points
  to: a body that reads the index and not the element carries no label
  of an element's value. A node of the same
  body that does not read the index lists no such slot and has none of
  that label, and a callback that declares the index and does not use it
  adds it to no template. The position is in no key: an element that
  moves keeps its key, and the nodes that read the index are evaluated
  again (section 1.3). A callback has no parameter for the
  whole array (`language-subset.md` §4.4.1). A body that needs the
  collection captures it by name, and the capture is an ordinary slot,
  like any other captured outer value.
- **Labels flow per value.** By ruling, the callback of a per-element
  construct is a pattern, and labels flow through it per value. Each
  thing the body is given has its own label. The element has the label
  of its own slot of the collection and of what that slot holds: the
  element's root slots and the slots below them, bound to position `i`.
  The index has the label of its slot, which is the label of the
  collection's array (section 2.2), and the whole collection the label
  of its capture, each only for a node that reads it.
  Each captured value has the label of its own slot or output of the
  enclosing instance. A node of the body takes the labels of what it
  reads and closes over, and nothing of what another node of the same
  body reads. A node is anything of the body that has a template: an
  output path, a `computed`, a `lift`, a handler, the argument of a
  child, the request of an operation. So a handler that closes over the
  element alone writes under the event and the element (section 3.12),
  also where another node of the body reads the index. Nothing of
  another element, and nothing of the collection's length or order,
  reaches a node that reads neither the index nor the collection. No
  label is formed for the callback as a whole, and none is stored for an
  element that a node of its body did not read. Section 2.2 says where
  the handle of the element and a captured handle are read. No place
  joins the labels of two positions: a key stands at one position, and
  what is stored for it carries that position's label (section 2.6).
- **A child.** A child that the body instantiates is per key (section
  1.3). That adds nothing to the element template: the body is not given
  the key and computes nothing from it.
- **Nothing else.** The label of element `i` does not include any slot of
  element `j`.

For a collection the instance computed (`Collection.source` of kind
`output`), a position has no stored address until the collection is kept.
The element's root slots then take the producing template: `shape` its
membership template, and `identity` the template of the reference at the
position. A slot below the root crosses that reference like any link
(section 2.5), with the producing template as the pointer's label. The
plan holds no copy of the producing template for this: the slots resolve
at run time to the label of the entry of `Plan.outputs` that has it,
which a transaction instantiates once and uses for every element and
every slot that resolves to it (section 4.1, "A label is instantiated
once").

A collection over a module-scope constant, or over an array literal
written in place, is a collection of this kind: the cone that yields the
array has an output for it, and `Collection.source` names that output.
For a constant, the membership template and the template of every
element are `const`. For a literal written in place, the membership is
the literal's `enumeration` and each position has the template of the
expression written there (section 3.4), so the element's root slots
resolve per position, as labels do (section 1.3). The elements of either
are plain values unless a position holds a reference. A state cell in
the body is per occurrence, as over any collection (section 1.3).

Element cones are keyed as section 1.3 defines, and the element slots are
bound per key, at the position that holds the key. The runtime, not the
value code, iterates: it evaluates
the body's cones once per key with that element's slots, and assembles the
result. Section 1.4 says which entry of `Plan.outputs` stands for the
assembled result. Which input element an output position came from is therefore
something the runtime knows, not something the value code reports.

This is the split of §8.5.6.1 (`08-05-collection-transitions.md`): "Child
paths like `/items/0` carry `shape` (membership/domain) and `value` (member
payload)."

**Today.** `map` (`runtime/runner/src/builtins/map.ts`) runs one sub-pattern
instance per element. The coordinator reads the list's membership and the
per-slot references but no element value, and its membership read is declared
onward (`listMembershipRead` in `list-coordinator-plan.ts`), so the container
carries membership and each element result carries its own element's label
plus its slot's ([CFC observation classes](../cfc-observation-classes.md) §6.2).
**Equal** for the `derived` part of the labels. The result container also holds
the static part of section 3.1: the stage 3 comparison observed, for a list that
has no label of its own and whose elements declare a clause, that the
container's root resolves to that clause, on a covering entry and on its
`enumerate` and `shape` entries. The covering entry is of origin `declared`.
The `enumerate` and `shape` entries are of origin `structure`: they hold the
join of the coordinator's transaction (`prepareBoundaryCommitSteps`; section
3.1), which is wider than the membership where that transaction consumed more
than the membership. The template of the container is the source's
`enumeration` slot, which carries neither. By ruling the template does not
join the static part, and the result's membership is the source's alone, so
the container is **tighter** than today with the `structure` entries compared
and without them, and the comparison expects that difference. Which read of
the coordinator's transaction consumes the clause of the elements was not
traced (section 8, question 70). The specification calls this arrangement
decomposition and prefers it (§8.5.4.3): "Each **element op** runs in its own transaction that
reads only its element." The template arrives at the same labels without the
transactions. Within one element's body, a `computed` that returns several paths
is **tighter** as in section 3.4.

**Today, the argument document of an element.** What an element's body is
given is stored in the argument document of the element's instance, and the
coordinator writes it. `reconcile` in `createMapInstance`
(`runtime/runner/src/builtins/map.ts`) runs in a transaction of its own and
sets up each element that has no run in that transaction
(`Runner.runInTransaction`), which writes the element's argument document.
`prepareBoundaryCommit` (`runtime/runner/src/cfc/prepare.ts`) computes one
join for the transaction (`deriveFlowJoin`) and stores it on every path the
transaction wrote. The prototype measured the result with the runner alone,
for a callback that declares neither the index nor the array and captures
two cells:

- **One join on every path.** The argument document
  `{ element, params: { center, zoom } }` has ten entries of origin
  `structure`: class `enumerate` and class `shape` at the root and at
  `params`, and class `followRef`, `shape` and `value` at `*` and at
  `params/*`. All ten hold the same clauses, the join of the coordinator's
  transaction. The link at `element` has one entry of origin `link` beside
  them, with the clause of the schema that the stored link carries
  (`linkSlotLabel`). Where that schema carries no clause the link has no
  such entry: in the comparison's run of
  `patterns/system/profile-picker/profile-picker.tsx`, whose input list
  declares its clause at the root of the list's cell, the argument
  document of an element has no entry of origin `link`, and the list's
  clause is on the entries of origin `structure`.
- **What the join holds.** The coordinator reads the whole raw array of the
  list once (`listMembershipRead` in
  `runtime/runner/src/builtins/list-coordinator-plan.ts`). The entries of
  class `shape` and `enumerate` at the list's own path go to the membership
  stamp of the result container and stay out of the join. Everything else
  that read consumes is joined: an entry with no class at the root, which
  is what a declared clause is, the entries at `*`, the entries at each
  slot, and the entries of everything stored in place below a slot. Where
  the slots hold links to a cell per element, the join has the list's
  declared label and no clause of an element's cell, and the `link` entry
  at `element` has the element's own. Where the elements are stored in
  place in the list's document, the join has the labels of every element.
  A reconcile that a change of the list started also reads the list as a
  trigger read (`addCfcTriggerReads`, called from `runSchedulerAction` in
  `runtime/runner/src/scheduler/run.ts`), and its join then has the list's
  own `shape` and `enumerate` entries as well.
- **What it does not hold.** `params` holds one link for each captured
  cell, and the coordinator reads no value of a captured cell, so no
  label of a captured cell is on an argument document. An element set up
  by a later reconcile gets the join of that reconcile, and the argument
  documents of the earlier elements are not written and keep theirs.
- **What a handler consumes.** A handler `zoom.set(14)` in an element body
  reads `params/zoom` of its element's argument document and nothing of
  the element, of another element, or of the list. It consumes the
  `followRef` entry at `params/*` and so stores the write under the
  coordinator's join. A handler that passes on a field of its element
  reads `element` and the field, and consumes the three entries at `*`
  and the `link` entry at `element` as well. A handler that does both in
  one body has one join for both writes.
- **With the index declared.** The argument document also holds `index`,
  with two entries of origin `derived` under the same join. Removing an
  earlier element writes `index` of the later elements again and no other
  path of their argument documents.

The template has none of the coordinator's join, by the ruling that labels
flow per value. It is **tighter** than today in two ways, both deliberate:
a handle the body was given carries no join of the coordinator, and no
label of one element reaches another where the elements are stored in
place. Section 3.1 has the comparison rule. Not measured: what the
argument document of an element of `filter` or of `flatMap` holds, what
changes when the callback declares the array, and the integrity of these
entries.

### 3.7 `filter` and `flatMap`

`xs.filter((x) => pred)` creates a derived `Collection`.

- **Membership template.** A `fold` whose `collection` is the record of the
  `filter` itself and whose `body` is the template of `pred`. The `fold`
  joins the membership the record iterates, which is the source's (section
  3.2). Which elements are present, and at which index, depends on the
  predicate's result for *every* element, dropped ones included.
- **Element template.** An element of the result is the source element,
  passed through: `slot` templates over the source's `element` root, so every
  class of integrity survives. Its root `shape` slot is replaced by the
  derived collection's membership template, because being at index `k` of the
  result depends on all the predicates.

- **The label of the array, for an index.** A body applied to the result
  that reads the index reads a slot of root `index` that names its own
  record, whose `source` names the record of the `filter` (section 2.2).
  The membership that record iterates is the `filter`'s membership
  template (section 3.2). The root of a position of the result is the
  root of the source element passed through: its `identity` slot, and
  its `shape`, which the membership template replaces. The label of the
  array is therefore the `filter`'s membership template, joined with the
  label of which reference each position of the result holds. It
  includes what every predicate read, because which elements the array
  holds depends on that. It includes a value behind a link only where a
  predicate read it. The same holds for the result of a `flatMap`, with
  its membership template and the roots of the elements the body
  returned, and for the result of a `map`, whose membership is its
  source's and whose positions have the roots the body's template gives
  them (section 3.6). By ruling the label is formed whole, and it joins
  nothing for the positions of the source that the predicate dropped
  beyond what the membership template holds.

`xs.flatMap((x) => body)`:

- **Membership template.** A `fold` whose `collection` is the record of the
  `flatMap` itself and whose `body` is the `enumeration` of the segment
  `body` returns. It joins the source's membership in the same way.
  Position and multiplicity depend on every segment's *length*, not on its
  content.
- **Element template.** The body's template for the originating element,
  with the root `shape` replaced by the membership template.

**Which element a position came from.** For both operations the runtime
evaluates the per-element cones (the predicate, or the body) and then performs
the structural step itself: it drops the elements whose predicate is falsy,
or concatenates the segments. The value code never builds the result
collection. The runtime records, with a derived collection, one fact per
source element: whether it was included, or the length of its segment. The
**origin** of each output position follows by prefix sum, and the runtime
binds the element slots of later templates through it. Nothing is reported by
emitted code and nothing needs
verifying, and element locality of these operations is a structural fact
(section 7.3).

**Labels flow per value** through the predicate of a `filter` and the
body of a `flatMap` as through the callback of a `map` (section 3.6): a
node of the callback takes the labels of what it reads and closes over,
the element has the label of its own slot of the source and of what that
slot holds, and the index has the source's `enumeration` only for a node
that reads it. The same holds for the callback of every other per-element
construct: the predicates of section 3.13 and the selector callbacks of
the aggregates and the indexes. What joins the labels of several elements
is the structural step, in the membership template above and in the rule
of each operation, and never the callback.

These follow §8.5.4.2, which separates membership, order and multiplicity
confidentiality from item content and notes that the two helpers "usually
still taint output positions by other elements even when each emitted item is
element-local".

**Today.** The `filter` coordinator (`runtime/runner/src/builtins/filter.ts`)
reads every predicate result, so all of them are in its one join, and
`recordCfcStructureContainer` has prepare mint the container's structure
entries from that join. Its output slots are links to the source elements.
**Equal.** The `flatMap` coordinator
(`runtime/runner/src/builtins/flatmap.ts`) reads every child *result*, so the
content label of every segment joins the container and the slots. The
template joins segment lengths only. **Tighter**, deliberately: this is the
precision §8.5.4.2 describes, and it rests on the compiler's claim that the
positions depend on lengths alone.

### 3.8 Aggregates

The aggregates are `count`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, `minBy` and `maxBy`, as
`builtin-inventory.md` lists them. `some`, `every` and `find` are reactive
constructs too; they depend on order and are in section 3.13.

| Aggregate | Template |
| --- | --- |
| `count()`, `.length` | The collection's membership |
| `count(predicate)` | `fold` of the predicate's template, joined with membership |
| `sum()`, `min()`, `max()` | `fold` of the element's `value`, joined with membership |
| `minBy(keyFunction)`, `maxBy(keyFunction)` | `pick` (section 3.18): the winning element, with the choice labeled by a `fold` of the key function's template |

`.length` reads the membership of the collection it is written on, and nothing
else. Its template is the `enumeration` slot at the collection's path, or the
`membership` of the collection's record where the instance computed the
collection. It is not a slot at a path `length` below the collection, of any
class: `length` is not a property the plan names a path for. That holds in
expression code and in a function body alike (`footprint-analysis.md` §2.2
and §3.4), so `computed(() => items.length)` has the `enumeration` slot at
`items` and no entry at `items/length`.

Where the instance computed the collection and no `Collection` record stands for
it, the template of `.length` is the template of the collection's own
`enumeration`, as the `output` row of the table in section 3.2 gives it: for an
assembled entry its `template`, for an array constructed in place the template
of its container entry (section 3.4), and for the result of one opaque call the
call's template. In each of the three the template of `.length` is the `output`
node that names that entry.

`.length` of a string is not an aggregate. A string has no membership, and its
length is computed from its content. For a string that is an input the template
is the `value` slot at the string's path, and for a string the instance computed
it is the template of the string. In both cases no path `length` is named.

A predicate is observed for truthiness, with the classes of section 3.5. The
callback of `minBy` and `maxBy` is called the **key function**: it returns
the key the elements are compared by. The callback of a collection index
(section 3.17) is a key function too.

**Semantics the plan fixes.** Value code on a client and on the server has
to agree, so the result of an aggregate is defined independently of how it is
computed.

- `sum` is exact: the result is the correctly rounded sum of the members,
  whatever their order (`AggregateSum` in
  `runtime/runner/src/builtins/aggregate-sum.ts` is the current
  implementation of that).
- The empty results are `0` for `sum` and `count`, `Infinity` for `min`,
  `-Infinity` for `max`, and `undefined` for `minBy` and `maxBy`.
- A tie in `minBy` or `maxBy` goes to the element at the first position, in
  the source order of the collection, among the elements whose key
  function returns the winning key. The result therefore depends on the
  order of the collection where keys tie. The choice is labeled with the
  collection's membership, which includes order (section 3.18), so the
  label covers it. No element key enters the choice.
- Equal elements count once each: each occurrence has a key of its own
  (section 1.3).
- A hole contributes nothing.

**Durable state.** An aggregate is an `Operation` of kind `aggregate`. Its
state holds one contribution per element key, the folded value, and the
multiset of label identifiers the
fold joins (section 4.3). A change to one element costs one update. A
reorder costs nothing for `count`, `sum`, `min` and `max`. For `minBy` and
`maxBy` it changes the result only where it changes which of the elements
with the winning key comes first, so the state also has to give the first
position among those. The shape of that state is private to the runtime;
only the semantics above are part of the design. Section 2.6 gives the
label of the state beside the result.

**Today.** `aggregate` (`runtime/runner/src/builtins/aggregate.ts`) builds a
tree of `aggregateNode` runs, each its own transaction, and labels accumulate
up the tree by the ordinary join. **Equal** for the value aggregates. For
`count` the coordinator reads the raw list; the template is the membership
alone. **Equal or tighter**, to be confirmed by the stage 3 comparison,
because what a raw list read consumes at its slots depends on the list's
stored entries. `minBy` and `maxBy` publish a link to the winning element
today. The link passes up the tree through node outputs, each labeled by a
transaction that read its members' key function results, so the choice
carries the join over all of them, as the `pick` template's choice does.
**Equal.**

### 3.9 Opaque sandboxed calls

A sandboxed body produces, for every path of its result and every path it
writes:

```text
derive(by: body) over
  slot r.slot        for each r in Body.reads
  c.template         for each c in Body.computed
  dynamic h          for each h in Body.handles
  dynamic link       for each journaled resolution of the body
  dynamic space      for each journaled access-list read of the body
  dynamic metadata   where the body has journaled label-metadata observations
```

The last three are the journaled context reads of section 3.16 ("Static
and journaled"), and each is an entry of `Plan.dynamicReads`.

**The argument.** The runtime builds the body's argument from `Body.reads`
and `Body.computed` and from nothing else. A slot that is not listed is not
materialized, so the body cannot observe it.

**Computed inputs.** A body can receive a value the instance computed, the
result of another body or of expression code: as an argument of a call in
the reactive tier, or as a capture of a body written there. Such a value
has a template and no slot. `Body.computed` lists what
the body observes of it, one entry per path and class, each with the
template of the producing expression at that path. Where the value is an
output of the plan, that template is the `output` node of the nearest
entry at or above the path, and where only the cone of the call computes
and uses the value, it is written in place (section 3.2, "A reference to
an output"). The cone's value
function passes the value, and the runtime copies into the argument the
paths the entries name, each narrowed to its class, as it
narrows a slot. The body's label joins the templates of the entries, and
not the template of the whole value.

An object or an array literal written in the reactive tier, as the
argument of a call or as a captured value, binds each member on its own.
What an input path is bound to is found by following the path into the
literal. Where it reaches a member that is a slot, or a path below one,
the body's entry there is a slot of `Body.reads`, with the member's root
and path. Where it reaches a member the instance computed, the entry is
an entry of `Body.computed` with that member's template. An entry at a
path of the literal itself, such as `enumeration` at the literal, is an
entry of `Body.computed` whose template is the literal's own (section
3.4).

A computed value passed whole would be looser than today. A body that
reads one member of an object the pattern body constructs reads that
member's document today and no other member's, so its label must not join
the other members' templates.

**Handles.** The runtime hands a body a cell handle for every position of
a handle type that its record names: an `identity` slot of `reads`, an
`identity` entry of `computed`, the handle of a write target or of a write
envelope, and every entry of `handles`. A handle the body finds through one
of those reaches it by the read that finds it. What the body can do with a
handle is bounded by the record:

- A read through the handle at a path that slots of `reads` cover returns
  the value the runtime materialized for those slots. `footprint-analysis.md`
  §7.2 says when a read through a handle is such a slot: the handle is one
  the body was given at a static place, the path below it is static, and
  every run that returns normally makes the read. The slot's path crosses
  the handle's link (section 2.5).
- A handle listed in `handles` reads through the transaction. Every read
  made through it is journaled, and it returns the value narrowed to the
  entry's `envelope`, so the journal holds the reads the envelope admits
  and no others. A read through it of a path that a slot also covers
  consumes that label a second time, which a join absorbs.
- A handle that is in neither group cannot be read through. It can be
  passed on, compared, and written through where a write target names it.
- A handle the body finds by a read through a listed handle has no entry
  of its own, because no slot names the place where it is. The body may
  read through it where the envelope of the listed entry admits the
  position as a handle. Finding it is a journaled read of the reference at
  that position. Reads through it are journaled with the reads of the entry
  it was found through, narrowed to what that entry's envelope admits
  below the position, and they join the same `dynamic` node. The same
  holds for a handle found through a found handle.
- A handle that `key` flattened is found in this sense where its use is
  not static. For `h` of type `Cell<{ a: Cell<T> }>`, a read through
  `h.key("a")` that is conditional, or through `h.key(k)` with a key the
  body computes, has no `get()` on `h`, and the runtime crosses the link
  at `a` when the flattened handle is used. That crossing is a journaled
  read of the reference at `a`, through the entry of `h` in `handles`,
  whose envelope admits the position `a` as a handle. The reads through
  the flattened handle are journaled under the same entry. Where the use
  is static, the hops are slots: `identity` at `h` and at `h->a`, and the
  slots of the read below them (section 2.5).
- A link to an instance that a `lift` or a `computed` made is a handle of
  this kind when the body reads through it. The instance outlives the
  evaluation that made it, so a later evaluation finds the child's result
